29110.e: Victoria married her cousin Albert in 1840. He was an important adviser. After his death in 1861 she wore mourning clothes for decades.

29111.q: Which great empire did Queen Victoria rule over?
29111.e: In Queen Victoria's time the British Empire was bigger than ever before. It included territories on every continent.
29111.m: Victoria ruled over the British Empire.

29112.q: What is the period of her reign called?
29112.e: The period was marked by industrialisation, strict moral ideas and the greatest extent of the British Empire.
29112.m: The Victorian era is named after Queen Victoria.

29113.q: Which extra title did Queen Victoria hold from 1876?
29113.e: In 1876 Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli had Victoria given the title “Empress of India”. It was meant to stress the importance of the most valuable colony.
29113.m: From 1876 Queen Victoria was also Empress of India.

29114.q: How many children did Queen Victoria have?
29114.e: Victoria had nine children. Many of them married into European royal families, which is why Victoria is called the “grandmother of Europe”.
29114.m: Victoria is called the “grandmother of Europe”.

29115.q: Around what time did Queen Victoria die?
29115.e: Victoria died in January 1901 on the Isle of Wight. The 20th century had just begun.

29116.q: Who became king after Queen Victoria's death?
29116.e: Her eldest son became king as Edward VII. He was already almost 60 years old. Her husband Albert had died back in 1861.

29117.q: Who did Karl Marx write the Communist Manifesto with?
29117.e: Engels was a close friend of Marx and wrote many works with him. As the son of a factory owner, he also supported Marx with money.
29117.m: Marx and Engels wrote the Manifesto together.

29118.q: In which year was the Communist Manifesto published?
29118.e: It was published in February 1848, shortly before several revolutions broke out. At first hardly anyone noticed it, but later it was translated into many languages.
29118.m: The Communist Manifesto was published in 1848.

29119.q: What did Marx and Engels demand in the Communist Manifesto?
a: Factories and machines should belong to everyone
Every family should own its own factory
29119.e: Marx and Engels wanted the means of production to belong not to a few rich people but to the whole of society. The workers were to unite for this.
29119.m: In the Manifesto, factories were to belong to everyone.

29120.q: According to the first sentence of the Manifesto, which “spectre” is haunting Europe?
29120.e: The Manifesto begins with the sentence “A spectre is haunting Europe, the spectre of communism.” Marx and Engels meant the fear of the powerful.
29120.m: The Manifesto begins with the spectre of communism.

29121.q: In Marx's writings, what is the class that owns the factories and machines called?
29121.e: The bourgeoisie owns the means of production. According to Marx, it is in a class struggle against the workers.
29121.m: In Marx's view the bourgeoisie owns the means of production.

29122.q: Which job did Karl Marx do besides his work as a thinker?
29122.e: Marx wrote for newspapers and in 1848/49 even ran a newspaper in Cologne. He earned part of his living by writing.
29122.m: Karl Marx also worked as a journalist.

29123.q: Which country did Karl Marx come from?
29123.e: Marx was born in Trier in 1818. Later he lived in exile, mainly in London.

29124.q: What is Karl Marx's main work, whose first volume came out in 1867, called?
29124.e: In this work, known in German as “Das Kapital”, Marx studied how the capitalist economy works. Engels published the further volumes after Marx's death.
29124.m: “Capital” is the main work of Karl Marx.

29125.q: In which city did Karl Marx live in exile from 1849 until his death?
29125.e: Marx was expelled from several countries and finally moved to London. There he did a lot of research in the library of the British Museum.
29125.m: Karl Marx spent his last decades in London.

29126.q: Which European country had the colonies of Angola and Mozambique in Africa?
29126.e: Portugal was one of the first European colonial powers in Africa. Angola and Mozambique only became independent in 1975.
29126.m: Angola and Mozambique were Portuguese colonies.

29127.q: Which African country defeated Italy in 1896 and stayed independent?
29127.e: Emperor Menelik II defeated the Italian army at Adwa. This made Ethiopia one of the few African countries that never became a colony.
29127.m: Ethiopia beat Italy in 1896 and stayed independent.

29128.q: Which colonial power wanted a land link from the Cape to Cairo?
29128.e: British people like Cecil Rhodes dreamed of a railway from Cape Town to Cairo through British territory. The plan was never fully carried out.
29128.m: Great Britain wanted to rule Africa from the Cape to Cairo.

29129.q: Which present-day country was the former colony of German South West Africa?
29129.e: German South West Africa was a German colony from 1884 to 1915. Today the state of Namibia is there.
29129.m: German South West Africa is today's Namibia.

29130.q: Which two colonial powers owned the most land in Africa?
29130.e: France ruled large parts of West and North Africa, and Great Britain many areas in the east and south. At Fashoda in Sudan the two even clashed in 1898.
29130.m: Great Britain and France were the biggest colonial powers in Africa.

29131.q: Against which colonial power did the Herero and Nama rise up in 1904?
29131.e: The Herero and Nama in German South West Africa fought back against land theft and oppression. The German way of waging war killed tens of thousands of people; today it is called genocide.
29131.m: The uprising of the Herero and Nama was brutally crushed by German troops.

29132.q: Who did the British fight against in the South African War from 1899 to 1902?
29132.e: The Boers were descendants mainly of Dutch settlers in South Africa. Great Britain defeated their republics and so won rich gold and diamond deposits.
29132.m: In the Boer War the British fought against the Boers in South Africa.

29133.q: Which European country conquered Algeria from 1830?
29133.e: France occupied Algiers in 1830 and made Algeria its most important colony. Algeria only became independent in 1962.

29134.q: In which city did the Congo Conference of 1884/85 take place?
29134.e: The representatives of the powers met in the Chancellery in the German capital. That is why it is also called the Berlin Conference.
29134.m: The Congo Conference met in Berlin.

29135.q: Which ruler received the Congo region as his personal property after the conference?
29135.e: The Congo did not belong to the Belgian state but to the king himself. His rule was notorious for its cruelty towards the people.
29135.m: The Congo Free State was the private property of King Leopold II.

29136.q: How many African representatives took part in the Congo Conference?
29136.e: Only European states, the USA and the Ottoman Empire negotiated about Africa. The people of Africa were not asked.
29136.m: No African was allowed to have a say at the Congo Conference.

29137.q: What was the territory on the Congo that became Leopold II's state in 1885 called?
29137.e: Despite its name, the so-called Congo Free State was not free. In 1908 the Belgian state took over the territory as the colony of the Belgian Congo.
29137.m: The Congo Free State belonged to Leopold II from 1885 to 1908.

29138.q: What did the European powers mainly want to settle at the Congo Conference?
a: How to divide Africa among themselves
How to give Africa its freedom
How to expand the slave trade
29138.e: The powers set rules for how they could take possession of territories in Africa. After that the continent was almost completely divided up.
29138.m: The Congo Conference was about dividing up Africa.

29139.q: Which continent had been almost completely divided up among European colonial powers by around 1900, after the Congo Conference?
29139.e: After 1885 the colonial powers took more and more territory in Africa. By around 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were still independent.
29139.m: By around 1900 Africa was almost completely divided into colonies.

29140.q: Because of the Belgian colonial period, which language is an official language in the Democratic Republic of the Congo today?
29140.e: French is one of the languages spoken in Belgium. The colonial rulers brought it to the Congo, where it is still an official language today.
29140.m: Because of the colonial period, French is spoken in the Congo.

29141.q: Which present-day country lies mostly on the territory of the former Congo Free State?
29141.e: Today's Democratic Republic of the Congo came out of the colony of the Belgian Congo in 1960. The Republic of the Congo to the west, on the other hand, was French.
29141.m: The Congo Free State was on the territory of today's Democratic Republic of the Congo.

29142.q: Which country did China fight in the First Opium War?
29142.e: China wanted to stop opium smuggling, but British traders were earning a lot from it. So Great Britain sent warships.
29142.m: In the First Opium War China fought against Great Britain.

29143.q: In which century did the Opium Wars take place?
29143.e: The First Opium War lasted from 1839 to 1842 and the Second from 1856 to 1860. So both took place in the 19th century.
29143.m: The Opium Wars took place in the 19th century.

29144.q: Which island did China have to give up in 1842?
29144.e: Hong Kong became a British colony. Only in 1997 did the city return to China.

29145.q: What did China have to do after the First Opium War?
a: Choose a new emperor from England
29145.e: In the peace treaty of 1842 China had to open several ports, give up Hong Kong and pay a lot of money.
29145.m: After the Opium War China had to open its ports.

29146.q: Why did China want to stop the opium trade?
a: Because China wanted to sell opium itself
29146.e: Opium is an addictive drug. More and more people in China became dependent on it, and a lot of silver flowed abroad.
29146.m: China wanted to stop the opium trade because of all the addicts.

29147.q: Who ruled China at the time of the Opium Wars?
29147.e: China was an empire at that time. The defeats in the Opium Wars greatly weakened the emperor's power.
29147.m: At the time of the Opium Wars China was ruled by an emperor.

29148.q: Which two countries fought against China in the Second Opium War?
29148.e: From 1856 to 1860 Great Britain and France fought a war against China together. In the end their troops even destroyed an imperial palace near Beijing.
29148.m: In the Second Opium War Great Britain and France fought against China.

29149.q: What does China call the treaties it was forced to sign in the 19th century?
29149.e: The treaties mainly benefited the foreign powers, for example with open ports and special rights for foreigners. China felt them as a humiliation.
29149.m: China calls the forced agreements “unequal treaties”.

29150.q: In which year did the Meiji Restoration begin in Japan?
29150.e: In 1868 the emperor was declared the real ruler of the country again. After that Japan modernised very quickly.

29151.q: Who lost his power through the Meiji Restoration?
29151.e: For over 250 years the shoguns of the Tokugawa family had ruled Japan. In 1868 power went back to the emperor.
29151.m: The Meiji Restoration ended the rule of the shoguns.

29152.q: Which country did the “Black Ships” that forced Japan to open its ports in 1853 come from?
29152.e: The American Commodore Matthew Perry appeared off the coast with his dark steamships. After that Japan had to sign treaties with the USA.
29152.m: American ships opened Japan to trade.

29153.q: What has the city of Edo been called since 1868?
29153.e: The emperor moved from Kyoto to Edo, which was renamed Tokyo. The name means “eastern capital”.
29153.m: Since 1868 Edo has been called Tokyo.

29154.q: Which warrior class lost its privileges in the Meiji period?
29154.e: The government introduced general military service and banned the samurai from carrying swords. A samurai uprising in 1877 failed.
29154.m: In the Meiji period the samurai lost their privileges.

29155.q: Where did Japan get ideas for railways, factories and a modern army in the Meiji period?
29155.e: Japanese experts travelled to Europe and America and studied technology, armies and constitutions there. For the constitution of 1889 they took Prussia as a model.
29155.m: In the Meiji period Japan learned from Europe and America.

29156.q: Which great power did Japan defeat in the war of 1904/05?
29156.e: In the Russo-Japanese War Japan won on land and at sea. For the first time in modern history an Asian state defeated a European great power in a major war.

29157.q: What mainly changed in Japan in the Meiji period?
a: Japan shut itself off completely from the world
29157.e: From 1868 Japan built railways, factories, schools and a modern army. Within a few decades it became a great power.
29157.m: In the Meiji period Japan quickly became modern.

29158.q: Which trading company ruled large parts of India until 1858?
29158.e: The East India Company had its own armies and governed huge territories. After the uprising of 1857 it lost its power.
29158.m: The East India Company ruled in India for a long time.

29159.q: Who rose up against British rule in India in 1857?
29159.e: The Indian soldiers of the British were called sepoys. In 1857 they mutinied, and the uprising spread across northern India.
29159.m: In 1857 Indian soldiers rose up against the British.

29160.q: Who ruled India directly from 1858, after the East India Company had lost its power?
29160.e: After the uprising of 1857 the British Crown itself took over the rule of India. This period is called the Raj, which means “rule” in Hindi.
29160.m: From 1858 the British Crown ruled India directly.

29161.q: What title did the highest representative of the British Crown in India hold?
29161.e: The viceroy governed in the name of the British monarch. He had great power in India.
29161.m: A viceroy represented the Crown in India.

29162.q: Which canal greatly shortened the sea route from Great Britain to India from 1869?
29162.e: The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea. Ships no longer had to sail all the way around Africa.
29162.m: The Suez Canal was Great Britain's shortest route to India.

29163.q: In which year did British rule over India end?
29163.e: On 15 August 1947 India became independent. At the same time the state of Pakistan was created.

29164.q: Which nickname did India have in the British Empire?
29164.e: India was Great Britain's most valuable colony. It provided raw materials, soldiers and a huge market.
29164.m: India was seen as the jewel in the British crown.

29165.q: Which Indian fought without violence for the independence of British India?
29165.e: Mahatma Gandhi called on Indians to resist without violence, for example with strikes and protest marches. In 1947 India became independent.
29165.m: Gandhi fought for India's independence without violence.

29166.q: From when to when did the Crimean War last?
29166.e: The war began in the Balkans in 1853 and soon spread to Crimea. It ended in 1856 with a peace treaty.
29166.m: The Crimean War lasted from 1853 to 1856.

29167.q: Which country did Great Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fight against in the Crimean War?
29167.e: Russia wanted to extend its influence over the weak Ottoman Empire. Great Britain and France wanted to prevent this.
29167.m: In the Crimean War Russia lost against an alliance.

29168.q: Which port city in Crimea was besieged for almost a year?
29168.e: Sevastopol was the base of the Russian Black Sea Fleet. The city fell in 1855 after a long siege.
29168.m: The siege of Sevastopol was at the heart of the Crimean War.

29169.q: Which peace treaty ended the Crimean War in 1856?
29169.e: In the Treaty of Paris the Black Sea was declared neutral for warships. Russia lost influence.
29169.m: The Crimean War ended with the Treaty of Paris.

29170.q: Which British nurse became famous in the Crimean War for caring for wounded soldiers?
29170.e: Florence Nightingale made the military hospitals cleaner and improved care. As a result far fewer soldiers died. She is seen as the founder of modern nursing.
29170.m: Florence Nightingale improved the care of the wounded in the Crimean War.

29171.q: Which nickname did Florence Nightingale get in the Crimean War?
29171.e: At night she walked through the wards with a lamp and visited the wounded soldiers. That is how she got her nickname.
29171.m: Florence Nightingale was the “Lady with the Lamp”.

29172.q: What did Florence Nightingale mainly improve in the military hospital?
29172.e: Conditions in the hospital were dirty and many wounded men died of disease. Nightingale made sure there was cleanliness, fresh linen and better care.
29172.m: Nightingale saved lives through cleanliness and good care.

29173.q: On which sea is the Crimean peninsula?
29173.e: Crimea juts into the Black Sea from the north. The Russian Black Sea Fleet was based in the port of Sevastopol, which is why there was heavy fighting there.
29173.m: Crimea is on the Black Sea.

29174.q: According to Florence Nightingale’s figures, what did most soldiers in the Crimean War die of?
29174.e: Nightingale counted the deaths carefully. She showed that far more soldiers died of disease than of wounds, and so she demanded cleaner hospitals.
29174.m: In the Crimean War more soldiers died of disease than of wounds.

29175.q: In which field did Florence Nightingale do pioneering work with diagrams?
29175.e: With colourful, circular diagrams she showed that more soldiers died of disease than of wounds. In this way she convinced politicians to make reforms.
29175.m: Nightingale used statistics to save lives.

29176.q: What is the name of the process by which the best adapted living things are more likely to survive and have offspring?
29176.e: According to Darwin, living things with useful features survive more often and pass these features on to their offspring. He called this process natural selection.
29176.m: Natural selection means that well adapted living things survive more often.

29178.q: What do we call the development of living things over a very long time, which Darwin studied?
29178.e: Darwin showed that living things change over many generations and that new species appear. This development is called evolution.
29178.m: Darwin explained the evolution of living things.

29179.q: Roughly how long did Darwin’s research voyage around the world last?
29179.e: The voyage began at the end of 1831 and ended in October 1836. Darwin spent most of the time on land doing research.
29179.m: Darwin’s voyage around the world lasted almost five years.

29180.q: Which book did Darwin publish in 1871, in which he also included humans in his theory?
29180.e: In this book Darwin explained that humans, too, developed from earlier living things. At the time this caused fierce debate.
29180.m: In 1871 Darwin wrote about the descent of man.

29181.q: Which country did Charles Darwin come from?
29181.e: Charles Darwin was born in England in 1809. He died in 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey in London.
29181.m: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist.

29182.q: Which animals did Darwin write his last book about in 1881?
29182.e: For decades Darwin watched how earthworms turn over the soil and create fertile earth. The book became a bestseller.
29182.m: Darwin showed how important earthworms are for the soil.

29183.q: What did Pasteur show with his experiments using glass flasks with long, curved necks?
a: Germs do not appear by themselves, they come from outside
Germs appear by themselves in any broth
Germs die even at room temperature
Germs only grow in the dark
29183.e: Many people believed that tiny living things could appear by themselves from dead matter. Using swan-neck flasks, Pasteur showed that germs only grow in boiled broth if they get in from outside.
29183.m: Pasteur proved that life does not simply appear by itself.

29184.q: What was Louis Pasteur trained as?
29184.e: Pasteur was a chemist, not a doctor. Even so, his discoveries are among the most important in medicine.
29184.m: The chemist Pasteur changed medicine, even though he was not a doctor.

29185.q: In 1881 Pasteur vaccinated part of a flock of sheep and then infected all the sheep with a disease. What happened?
29185.e: At Pouilly-le-Fort Pasteur vaccinated part of the flock against anthrax. When all were infected with the germ, only the vaccinated animals survived. This made vaccination famous.
29185.m: Pasteur’s experiment with sheep showed that vaccination protects.

29186.q: From 1865, which animals did Pasteur help by studying a disease that threatened French silk production?
29186.e: At that time a disease was killing many silkworms. Pasteur found out how to recognise sick animals and remove them.
29186.m: With his research Pasteur saved silkworm farming in France.

29187.q: What do we call protecting someone against a disease with weakened germs?
29187.e: Around 1880 Pasteur discovered in chickens that old, weakened germs protect against the disease. This idea became the basis of many vaccinations.
29187.m: Weakened germs can protect against a disease.

29188.q: Edward Jenner protected people against smallpox by vaccinating them with cowpox. Which animal does the word “vaccine” therefore come from?
29188.e: The Latin word for cow is vacca. In honour of Jenner, Pasteur called all such protective substances “vaccines”.
29188.m: The word vaccine reminds us of the cow.

29189.q: Against which dangerous disease, often passed on by dog bites, did Pasteur develop a vaccine in 1885?
29189.e: In 1885 Pasteur vaccinated a boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog. The boy survived. This made Pasteur famous all over the world.
29189.m: Pasteur developed a vaccine against rabies.

29190.q: Which group of germs does the cause of tuberculosis belong to?
29190.e: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium that often attacks the lungs. After its discoverer it is also called Koch’s bacillus.
29190.m: Tuberculosis is a disease caused by bacteria.

29191.q: What did Robert Koch hope he had found in 1890?
29191.e: In 1890 Koch presented a substance that was supposed to cure tuberculosis. But it did not work as hoped and today it is only used for a skin test.
29191.m: Koch searched for a long time for a cure for tuberculosis.

29192.q: What did Robert Koch prove with his research?
a: That certain bacteria cause certain diseases
That diseases come from bad air
That diseases come from the stars
29192.e: Koch showed, for example, that tuberculosis and cholera are caused by very specific bacteria. This meant people could fight diseases in a targeted way.
29192.m: Koch proved that bacteria cause diseases.

29193.q: Which flat glass dish for growing bacteria is named after one of Robert Koch’s assistants?
29193.e: Julius Richard Petri worked in Koch’s laboratory and introduced the dish in 1887. It is still used in every laboratory today.
29193.m: The Petri dish comes from Robert Koch’s laboratory.

29194.q: With which instrument did Robert Koch study the tiny bacteria?
29194.e: Bacteria are so small that you cannot see them with the naked eye. Koch could only see them under the microscope.
29194.m: You can only see bacteria under a microscope.

29195.q: What was Koch one of the first to use to record bacteria accurately?
29195.e: Koch photographed bacteria through the microscope. This allowed other researchers to check his findings carefully.
29195.m: Koch made bacteria visible to everyone with photos.

29196.q: With which French scientist did Koch have a famous rivalry over discoveries?
29196.e: Koch and Pasteur were the two leading bacteria researchers of their time. They argued fiercely, partly because Germany and France were enemies.
29196.m: Koch and Pasteur were great rivals in bacteria research.

29197.q: In which two subjects did Marie Curie win a Nobel Prize?
29197.e: She won the physics prize together with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, and the chemistry prize on her own. She is still the only person with Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
29197.m: Marie Curie was honoured in both physics and chemistry.

29198.q: Who did Marie Curie share her first Nobel Prize with?
29198.e: In 1903 she won the Nobel Prize in Physics together with her husband Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. Her second Nobel Prize followed eight years later.
29198.m: Marie Curie won her first Nobel Prize with her husband Pierre.

29199.q: Which chemical element was named in honour of Marie and Pierre Curie?
29199.e: The artificial element with atomic number 96 was first made in 1944. Its name, curium, honours the two scientists.
29199.m: The element curium bears the name of the Curies.

29200.q: What did Marie Curie do in 1906 as the first woman at the Sorbonne in Paris?
a: She became head of the university
29200.e: After her husband died in an accident, she took over his teaching duties and gave her first lecture in November 1906. In 1908 she became a full professor.
29200.m: Marie Curie was the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne.

29201.q: Which member of Marie Curie’s family also won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1935?
29201.e: Irène Joliot-Curie was honoured together with her husband for making artificial radioactive substances. The Curies are one of the most successful families of scientists.
29201.m: Marie Curie’s daughter Irène also won a Nobel Prize.

29202.q: Which country did Marie Curie come from?
29202.e: Marie Curie was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867. She moved to Paris to study, where she married Pierre Curie.

29203.q: Which new element did Marie and Pierre Curie discover in 1898?
29203.e: In 1898 the Curies discovered the elements polonium and radium. To do this they processed tonnes of rock and got only tiny amounts.
29203.m: The Curies discovered the element radium.

29205.q: What did Röntgen give up so that everyone could use his discovery freely?
29205.e: Röntgen did not apply for a patent and earned no money from his discovery. This meant hospitals all over the world could quickly use the rays.
29205.m: Röntgen gave his discovery to the whole world by not applying for a patent.

29206.q: What was Röntgen experimenting with when he discovered the new rays?
a: With a glass tube with electricity flowing through it
29206.e: Röntgen was studying a glass tube in which electric current flowed through an almost airless space. The invisible rays came from this tube.
29206.m: Röntgen discovered the rays during experiments with an electrified glass tube.

29207.q: In which country was Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen born?
29207.e: Röntgen was born in 1845 in Lennep, which is now part of Remscheid in Germany. Later he studied in Zurich.

29208.q: In which country did Röntgen grow up?
29208.e: When Röntgen was three years old, his family moved to Apeldoorn in the Netherlands. His mother was Dutch.
29208.m: Röntgen spent his childhood in the Netherlands.

29209.q: What did Röntgen notice first that made him aware of the unknown rays?
29209.e: Even though his experimental tube was covered with black cardboard, a screen nearby glowed. Invisible rays must have passed through the cardboard.
29209.m: A glowing screen revealed the invisible rays to Röntgen.

29210.q: Which chemical element is named after Röntgen?
29210.e: The artificially made element 111 was named after him in 2004. It decays very quickly.
29210.m: The element roentgenium honours Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen.

29211.q: In which year did Einstein publish his special theory of relativity?
29211.e: 1905 is known as Einstein’s miracle year because he published several groundbreaking papers. The general theory of relativity followed ten years later.
29211.m: The special theory of relativity dates from 1905.

29212.q: In which Swiss canton did Einstein pass his school leaving exam, the Matura, in 1896?
29212.e: Einstein attended the cantonal school in Aarau in the canton of Aargau. After that he studied in Zurich.
29212.m: Einstein took his Matura in Aarau in the canton of Aargau.

29213.q: Which famous prize did Albert Einstein receive for the year 1921?
29213.e: Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics. He was honoured for explaining how light knocks electrons out of metal, not for the theory of relativity.
29213.m: Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

29214.q: To which US president did Einstein write a letter in 1939 warning of a German atomic bomb?
29214.e: The physicist Leo Szilard wrote the letter and Einstein signed it. Later Einstein regretted this step.
29214.m: In 1939 Einstein warned President Roosevelt of a German atomic bomb.

29215.q: What was special about Einstein’s first wife, Mileva Marić?
a: She was one of the few women studying physics
She was a member of the Federal Council
29215.e: Mileva Marić studied with Einstein at the Polytechnic in Zurich. At that time very few women studied physics.
29215.m: Einstein’s first wife Mileva Marić studied physics.

29216.q: In which Swiss city can you visit Einstein’s former flat as a museum?
29216.e: Einstein lived on the Kramgasse in Bern’s old town from 1903 to 1905. Today the Einstein House is there.
29216.m: The Einstein House is in Bern.

29217.q: Why did Einstein not return to Germany in 1933 and stay in the USA instead?
a: Because as a Jew he was persecuted by the Nazis
Because he wanted to become president of America
Because he had won the lottery there
29217.e: After Hitler seized power, Jews in Germany were persecuted. Einstein stayed in the USA and did research in Princeton until his death in 1955.
29217.m: Einstein left Germany in 1933 because of the Nazis.

29218.q: Where did Einstein work in Bern when he wrote his famous papers in 1905?
29218.e: Einstein examined inventions at the Federal Patent Office. In his free time he wrote the papers that made him famous.
29218.m: Einstein worked at the patent office in Bern.

29219.q: What was Samuel Morse’s job before he took up the telegraph?
29219.e: Samuel Morse was a well-known American painter. Only later did he turn to electricity and develop his telegraph.
29219.m: The inventor of Morse code was originally a painter.

29220.q: What is the distress signal SOS in Morse code?
29220.e: S is made of three short signals and O of three long ones. The distress signal is easy to send and easy to recognise.
29220.m: SOS in Morse is three short, three long and three short signals.

29221.q: In which country did Samuel Morse send his first official telegraph message in 1844?
29221.e: The message went from Washington to Baltimore. After that the telegraph spread quickly.
29221.m: The first Morse line was built in the USA in 1844.

29222.q: How were messages sent with the electric telegraph?
29222.e: In the electric telegraph, pulses of electricity flow through a wire. As early as 1833 Gauss and Weber built such a line in Göttingen.
29222.m: The electric telegraph sends messages with electricity through wires.

29223.q: What did the railways soon use the telegraph for?
29223.e: With the telegraph one station could tell the next that a train was on its way. This prevented accidents.
29223.m: The telegraph made the railways safer.

29224.q: How are letters shown in Morse code?
29224.e: Each letter is made of short and long signals. Samuel Morse and his assistant Alfred Vail developed the code.
29224.m: Morse code is made of short and long signals.

29225.q: Who was responsible for telegraphy in Switzerland from 1851?
29225.e: In 1851 the federal government made telegraphy a federal matter. The first line, between Zurich and St Gallen, opened as early as 1852.
29225.m: In Switzerland telegraphy was a matter for the federal government.

29226.q: What does the Greek word “photography” roughly mean?
29226.e: The word is made up of the Greek words for light and for writing or drawing. In a photograph, light creates the picture.
29226.m: Photography really means drawing with light.

29227.q: Which process did William Henry Fox Talbot develop that allowed many prints to be made from one picture?
29227.e: Talbot first created a negative on paper. From this, as many positive prints as you liked could be made, which was not possible with the daguerreotype.
29227.m: Thanks to Talbot’s negative, a photo could be printed many times.

29228.q: What is the name of the dark room with a small hole that projects a picture onto the back wall and is seen as the forerunner of the camera?
29228.e: Camera obscura means dark room. Light comes in through the hole and creates an upside-down picture of the surroundings.
29228.m: The camera obscura is the earliest form of every camera.

29229.q: Which French brothers brought out the first practical process for colour photos, the autochrome, in 1907?
29229.e: Auguste and Louis Lumière used tiny dyed grains of starch as colour filters. They are also known as pioneers of cinema.
29229.m: The Lumière brothers made colour photos possible for many people.

29230.q: What was different about a daguerreotype compared with later photos?
a: Each picture was one of a kind.
The pictures were always in colour.
You could look at them on a mobile phone.
You could make as many prints as you liked.
29230.e: The daguerreotype was made directly on a metal plate. It could not be copied, so each picture existed only once.
29230.m: A daguerreotype is a single picture on a metal plate.

29231.q: What made taking photos easy for many people from 1888?
29231.e: George Eastman sold a small camera with roll film, which you sent away to be developed after taking your photos. This meant amateurs could take photos too.
29231.m: With roll film, photography became a hobby for everyone.

29232.q: What does the first photo in which a person can be seen probably show?
a: A man having his shoes shined in Paris
A family in front of their house
29232.e: In 1838 Louis Daguerre photographed the Boulevard du Temple in Paris. Only a man who stood still for a long time to have his shoes shined remained visible in the picture.
29232.m: One of the first photos shows a man having his shoes shined.

29233.q: What was the name of the place in New Jersey where Edison ran his famous invention laboratory?
29233.e: Many of Edison’s inventions were made in Menlo Park. That is why he was also called “the Wizard of Menlo Park”.
29233.m: Edison was known as the Wizard of Menlo Park.

29234.q: Which type of current did Edison want to win out in the so-called War of the Currents?
29234.e: Edison backed direct current, while his rivals Westinghouse and Tesla backed alternating current. In the end alternating current won for power grids.
29234.m: In the War of the Currents, Edison’s direct current lost to alternating current.

29235.q: What did Edison open on Pearl Street in New York in 1882?
29235.e: The power station supplied homes and offices in Manhattan with electricity. It was one of the first public power stations in the world.
29235.m: Edison built one of the first public power stations.

29236.q: Which device for watching short films did Edison’s company develop in the early 1890s?
29236.e: With the kinetoscope, one person looked through a peephole at a moving strip of film. It was a forerunner of the cinema.
29236.m: The kinetoscope showed moving pictures even before the cinema.

29237.q: What disability had Edison had since his youth?
29237.e: Edison had been almost deaf since his youth. He said that this helped him to concentrate better.
29237.m: Edison was hard of hearing and still a great inventor.

29238.q: What job did Edison do as a young man?
29238.e: As a teenager Edison worked as a telegraph operator in various places. His first invention was an electric vote-counting machine.
29238.m: The young Edison worked as a telegraph operator.

29239.q: According to a well-known quote by Edison, genius is one per cent inspiration. What percentage is perspiration?
29239.e: Edison meant that hard work is more important than a good idea. One per cent plus 99 per cent makes 100 per cent.
29239.m: For Edison, success was above all hard work.

29240.q: What kind of engine powered Carl Benz’s motor car?
29240.e: Benz used a single-cylinder four-stroke engine that ran on light petrol. Rudolf Diesel only invented the diesel engine a few years later.
29240.m: Benz’s first car was powered by a petrol engine.

29241.q: Which country did the car pioneer Carl Benz come from?
29241.e: Carl Benz was born in Karlsruhe in 1844 and built his first car in Mannheim.

29242.q: Roughly how much power did the engine of the first Benz motor car have?
29242.e: The single-cylinder engine produced about three quarters of a horsepower. A modern car often has more than a hundred times as much.
29242.m: The first motor car had less power than a horse.

29243.q: Which car brand today bears Carl Benz’s name?
29243.e: In 1926 the companies of Benz and Daimler merged to form Daimler-Benz AG. Their cars are still called Mercedes-Benz today.
29243.m: The Mercedes-Benz brand reminds us of Carl Benz.

29244.q: Who made the first long car journey in Carl Benz’s motor car in 1888?
29244.e: In 1888 Bertha Benz drove with her two sons from Mannheim to Pforzheim. She showed that the car worked in everyday life.
29244.m: Bertha Benz made the first long car journey in 1888.

29246.q: Where did Bertha Benz buy fuel on her long car journey in 1888?
29246.e: There were no petrol stations yet. The fuel ligroin, a light petrol, was sold in chemists’ shops as a cleaning product. Bertha Benz bought some in Wiesloch.
29246.m: In 1888 Bertha Benz filled up at a chemist’s.

29247.q: Near which place in North Carolina did the Wright brothers’ first powered flight take place?
29247.e: At Kitty Hawk there was a steady wind, and the sand dunes offered soft landing places. Strictly speaking, they flew at the Kill Devil Hills near the town.
29247.m: The Wrights first flew near Kitty Hawk.

29248.q: How did the Wright brothers earn their money before they built aeroplanes?
29248.e: The brothers had a bicycle workshop. There they learned a lot about light construction and balance, which helped them build aeroplanes.
29248.m: The Wright brothers were first bicycle mechanics.

29249.q: In which month did the Wright brothers’ first powered flight take place?
29249.e: The flight succeeded on 17 December. On that cold day a strong wind was blowing.
29249.m: The first powered flight took place on a December day.

29250.q: How long did the longest of the four flights on the day of the first powered flight last?
29250.e: On the fourth attempt Wilbur Wright flew about 260 metres. Afterwards a gust of wind damaged the aeroplane.
29250.m: The longest flight on the first day lasted just under a minute.

29251.q: What tool did the Wrights build in 1901 to test many wing shapes?
29251.e: In a home-made wind tunnel they measured the lift and air resistance of about 200 model wings. This helped them find better wing shapes.
29251.m: The Wrights tested their wings in a wind tunnel.

29252.q: How did the Wrights steer their aeroplane into a turn?
29252.e: Using cords, they bent the wing tips slightly so that the aeroplane tilted to the side. This wing warping was a forerunner of today’s ailerons.
29252.m: The Wrights steered their aeroplane by bending the wings.

29253.q: What design did the Wright brothers’ first powered aeroplane have?
29253.e: The aeroplane had two wings of wood and fabric, one above the other. This design made it light and stable.
29253.m: The first powered aeroplane was a biplane.

29254.q: Why could many families afford Ford’s Model T?
a: It was built cheaply on an assembly line.
The state gave it to every family.
It was made of wood and paper.
29254.e: On the assembly line the cars were made quickly and in large numbers. As a result the Model T became cheaper and cheaper, and many families bought one.
29254.m: The assembly line made the Model T cheap.

29255.q: Roughly how many Model T cars were built in total?
29255.e: From 1908 to 1927 more than 15 million were built. For a long time it was one of the most produced cars in the world.
29255.m: About 15 million Model T cars were made.

29256.q: Which car did Henry Ford build in large numbers on an assembly line from 1913?
29256.e: The Model T was simple and sturdy. Thanks to the assembly line, over 15 million were built.
29256.m: Ford’s Model T was the first car for many people.

29257.q: Roughly how long did it take to assemble a chassis after the assembly line was introduced?
a: About an hour and a half
29257.e: Before, it took over twelve hours to build a chassis. With the assembly line it took about 93 minutes.
29257.m: The assembly line hugely shortened the time needed to build a car.

29258.q: Where did Ford get the idea for the assembly line?
29258.e: In the slaughterhouses the animals hung on hooks and moved from worker to worker. Ford applied this principle to building cars.
29258.m: The idea of the assembly line came from the slaughterhouses of Chicago.

29259.q: In the company of which famous inventor did Ford work as an engineer before he built cars?
29259.e: Ford was chief engineer at one of Edison’s electricity companies in Detroit. Edison encouraged him to keep working on his car.
29259.m: Henry Ford first worked for one of Thomas Edison’s companies.

29260.q: Why could many workers afford their own car thanks to Henry Ford?
a: The assembly line made cars cheaper
The state gave everyone a car
29260.e: With the assembly line Ford built cars much faster and more cheaply. So the price fell, and even his own workers could buy a car.
29260.m: The assembly line made the car affordable for many.

29261.q: Roughly how many people died when the Titanic sank?
29261.e: Of about 2200 people on board, over 1500 died. Only about 700 people survived.
29261.m: More than 1500 people died when the Titanic sank.

29262.q: How were the survivors of the Titanic rescued?
a: Another ship picked them up from the lifeboats
29262.e: The ship Carpathia received the distress calls and hurried there. It only arrived after the sinking and took the people from the boats.
29262.m: The Carpathia rescued the survivors of the Titanic.

29263.q: In which year was the wreck of the Titanic found on the seabed?
29263.e: A team led by the ocean explorer Robert Ballard found the wreck in 1985 at a depth of about 3800 metres. It lies on the bottom in two large pieces.
29263.m: The wreck of the Titanic was discovered in 1985.

29264.q: What was the Titanic when it set sail in 1912?
a: The largest ship in the world
29264.e: The Titanic was built in Belfast. At the time it was the largest ship in the world and was thought to be unsinkable.
29264.m: The Titanic was the largest ship of its time.

29265.q: Where was the Titanic supposed to go on its first voyage?
29265.e: The Titanic left Southampton in England in April 1912. Its destination was New York, but it never arrived there.
29265.m: The Titanic was on its way to New York.

29266.q: What happened to the captain of the Titanic?
a: He was the first to save himself
He was not on board at all
29266.e: Captain Edward Smith was very experienced and was supposed to retire after the voyage. He died in the sinking.
29266.m: The captain of the Titanic went down with his ship.

29267.q: Roughly how long was the Titanic?
29267.e: At about 269 metres it was longer than two football pitches end to end. At the time it was the largest moving structure.
29267.m: The Titanic was about 270 metres long.

29268.q: Roughly how much time passed between the collision and the sinking of the Titanic?
29268.e: The collision happened at 11.40 pm, and the ship sank at 2.20 am. During this time the lifeboats were lowered into the water.
29268.m: The Titanic sank in less than three hours.

29269.q: About how long did it take after its discovery in 1928 until penicillin was produced in large amounts as a medicine?
29269.e: Fleming discovered the substance in 1928 but could not make it in pure form. Only other researchers found a way, and from about 1943 there were large amounts.
29269.m: It took about 15 years until penicillin was available as a medicine.

29270.q: In which city was Fleming working when he discovered penicillin?
29270.e: Fleming did his research at St Mary’s Hospital in London. Today you can visit his laboratory there as a small museum.
29270.m: Penicillin was discovered in a hospital in London.

29272.q: What is the name of the genus of mould from which Fleming obtained his substance?
29272.e: The mould Penicillium gave the substance its name. The name comes from the Latin word for paintbrush, because the mould looks like one under the microscope.
29272.m: The name penicillin comes from the brush mould Penicillium.

29273.q: In which war was penicillin first produced and used in large amounts?
29273.e: From 1943, mainly companies in the USA produced large amounts. Many wounded soldiers survived their infections thanks to the medicine.
29273.m: In the Second World War penicillin saved many lives.

29274.q: What did Fleming already warn about in his Nobel Prize speech in 1945?
29274.e: Fleming warned that bacteria become resistant if the medicine is taken for too short a time or in too weak a dose. Such resistance is a big problem today.

29275.q: What did Fleming notice in 1928 around a patch of mould on his dish of bacteria?
a: No bacteria grew there any more
The bacteria grew twice as fast there
The dish glowed in the dark there
29275.e: Before his holiday Fleming had left dishes of bacteria standing. By chance a mould grew on one, and around it the bacteria died.
29275.m: A mould kept the bacteria away on Fleming’s dish.

29276.q: Who was shot in the assassination in Sarajevo?
29276.e: The man killed was Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary. He was visiting Sarajevo for military manoeuvres.
29276.m: The Austrian heir to the throne Franz Ferdinand died in the assassination in Sarajevo.

29277.q: In which year did the assassination in Sarajevo take place?
29277.e: The assassination happened on 28 June 1914. It is seen as the trigger of the First World War, which began that same summer.
29277.m: The assassination in Sarajevo happened in the summer of 1914.

29278.q: What was the name of the assassin in Sarajevo?
29278.e: The 19-year-old Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip fired the fatal shots. Because he was not yet 20, he escaped the death penalty.
29278.m: Gavrilo Princip shot the heir to the throne and his wife in Sarajevo.

29279.q: On the morning of the assassination in Sarajevo, what did a fellow conspirator first try to kill the heir to the throne with?
29279.e: Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb at the heir’s car. It bounced off and injured people in the car behind.
29279.m: The first attack in Sarajevo, with a bomb, failed.

29280.q: What did the young assassins in Sarajevo want to achieve?
a: Bosnia should no longer belong to Austria-Hungary.
Bosnia should become part of France.
The heir to the throne should become emperor.
29280.e: The assassins were young nationalists. They wanted Bosnia to be free of Austria-Hungary and to unite with Serbia and other South Slavs.
29280.m: The assassins wanted to separate Bosnia from Austria-Hungary.

29281.q: On which country did Austria-Hungary declare war one month after the assassination in Sarajevo?
29281.e: Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia for the assassination and issued an ultimatum. The declaration of war followed on 28 July 1914.
29281.m: Austria-Hungary started the war by declaring war on Serbia.

29282.q: Which country fought on the side of Austria-Hungary in the First World War?
29282.e: After the assassination, the German Empire promised Austria-Hungary its full support. France, Great Britain and Russia fought on the other side.
29282.m: Germany and Austria-Hungary fought together in the First World War.

29283.q: Sarajevo is the capital of which country today?
29283.e: Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1914 the area belonged to Austria-Hungary.
29283.m: Sarajevo is now the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

29284.q: In which year did the Battle of Verdun begin?
29284.e: The battle began in February 1916 and lasted until December of the same year.
29284.m: The Battle of Verdun raged for almost the whole of 1916.

29285.q: Which two armies mainly fought each other in the Battle of Verdun?
29285.e: The German army attacked the French fortress town of Verdun. The French defended it with huge losses.
29285.m: At Verdun, Germany and France fought each other.

29286.q: On which river is the town of Verdun?
29286.e: Verdun lies in north-eastern France on the Meuse. The fighting took place on both sides of the river.
29286.m: The fortress town of Verdun lies on the Meuse.

29287.q: What does Verdun stand for today?
a: The reconciliation of Germany and France
The start of the Second World War
29287.e: In 1984 the German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and the French President François Mitterrand held hands at Verdun. The picture became a symbol of friendship between the two countries.
29287.m: Verdun is now a place of German and French reconciliation.

29288.q: Roughly how long did the Battle of Verdun last?
29288.e: The battle began in February 1916 and ended in December 1916. Despite the long fighting, the front hardly moved.
29288.m: The Battle of Verdun lasted almost the whole of 1916.

29289.q: What protected the town of Verdun from attacks?
a: A wide arm of the sea
29289.e: Around Verdun there were many forts, that is, fortresses. The strongest, Fort Douaumont, fell to the Germans in February 1916.

29290.q: How was Verdun mainly supplied during the battle?
29290.e: Day and night, lorries carried soldiers, ammunition and food to Verdun. The French called this road the “Sacred Way”.
29290.m: Lorries supplied Verdun along a single road.

29291.q: What nickname did the Battle of Verdun get because of the many dead?
29291.e: In a small area about 300,000 soldiers died, and many more were wounded. That is why people speak of the “Hell of Verdun”.
29291.m: The Battle of Verdun is often called the “Hell of Verdun”.

29292.q: Which later author of “The Lord of the Rings” fought as a British officer at the Somme in 1916?
29292.e: Tolkien served as a signals officer and fell ill with trench fever in autumn 1916. Many researchers see traces of his war experiences in his books.
29292.m: J. R. R. Tolkien experienced the Battle of the Somme as a soldier.

29293.q: Which armies attacked the German positions at the Somme?
29293.e: The Somme offensive was a joint attack by Great Britain and France. It was also meant to take pressure off the French at Verdun.
29293.m: At the Somme the British and French attacked together.

29294.q: Which army suffered the heaviest losses in a single day in its history on the first day of the Battle of the Somme?
29294.e: On 1 July 1916 the British army lost about 57,000 men killed, wounded and missing, including about 19,000 dead.
29294.m: The first day of the Somme was the British army’s worst day for losses.

29295.q: Which new weapon did the British use for the first time at the Somme in September 1916?
29295.e: On 15 September 1916, near Flers-Courcelette, British tanks went into battle for the first time. But many got stuck or broke down.
29295.m: Tanks were used for the first time in the Battle of the Somme.

29296.q: In which country does the Somme, where fighting took place in 1916, flow?
29296.e: The Somme is a river in northern France. In the First World War the front ran there.
29296.m: The Battle of the Somme took place in northern France.

29297.q: What do we call the ditches in which the soldiers at the Somme lived and fought?
29297.e: In the First World War the armies dug themselves into long trenches. The soldiers often lived there for months in mud and cold.
29297.m: At the Somme the soldiers fought from trenches.

29298.q: What came before the attack at the Somme for a whole week?
29298.e: For a week the artillery shelled the German lines. But the barbed wire and the deep dugouts were often not destroyed.
29298.m: Before the Somme offensive the artillery fired for a week.

29299.q: How many soldiers in total were killed, wounded or missing in the Battle of the Somme?
29299.e: By the end in November 1916, all sides together counted over a million dead, wounded and missing. The front moved only a few kilometres.
29299.m: The Battle of the Somme was one of the costliest battles in history.

29300.q: What do we call a way of fighting in which the front lines in trenches hardly move?
29300.e: From the end of 1914 the armies dug in on the Western Front. For years the front hardly moved; this is called trench warfare.
29300.m: In trench warfare the front lines hardly move.

29301.q: What was the area between the enemy trenches called?
29301.e: The ground between the trenches belonged to neither side. Anyone who entered it immediately came under fire.
29301.m: Between the trenches lay the dangerous no man’s land.

29302.q: What was used as extra protection for trenches against attacking soldiers?
29302.e: Thick rolls of barbed wire were laid out in front of the trenches. Attackers got caught in them and were easy targets.
29302.m: Barbed wire protected the trenches from attackers.

29303.q: Which condition did soldiers get when their feet stayed wet and cold in the trench for a long time?
29303.e: With trench foot, tissue dies because of wet and cold. In the worst cases toes or feet had to be amputated.
29303.m: Wet and cold feet in the trenches led to trench foot.

29304.q: Which terrible new weapon was first used on a large scale in the First World War in 1915?
29304.e: On 22 April 1915 chlorine gas was released near Ypres in Belgium. After that, gas masks were part of the equipment in the trenches.
29304.m: In 1915 poison gas was used on a large scale for the first time in the First World War.

29305.q: To which national border did the trenches of the Western Front reach in the south?
29305.e: The Western Front stretched for about 700 kilometres from the North Sea coast in Belgium to the Swiss border near Pfetterhouse in Alsace.
29305.m: The Western Front ended at the border with Switzerland.

29306.q: What is the name of the spontaneous ceasefire on the Western Front at Christmas 1914?
29306.e: In some parts of the front, soldiers on both sides sang songs, exchanged gifts and buried their dead. The army commanders banned such meetings afterwards.
29306.m: In the Christmas truce of 1914 the guns fell silent on parts of the front.

29307.q: In which year did the USA enter the First World War?
29307.e: On 6 April 1917 the United States Congress declared war on the German Empire.
29307.m: The USA entered the First World War in 1917.

29308.q: Which US president led the USA into the First World War?
29308.e: Woodrow Wilson was president from 1913 to 1921. For a long time he had relied on neutrality, but in 1917 he asked Congress to declare war.
29308.m: President Woodrow Wilson led the USA into the war in 1917.

29309.q: Which ocean did American soldiers have to cross in 1917 to fight in Europe?
29309.e: The US soldiers were taken by ship across the Atlantic to France. German submarines tried to sink these transports.
29309.m: The US troops came to Europe across the Atlantic.

29310.q: Which German way of fighting at sea greatly contributed to the USA entering the war in 1917?
29310.e: From February 1917 German submarines also sank ships of neutral countries without warning. American ships were hit.
29310.m: Unrestricted submarine warfare turned the USA against Germany.

29311.q: Which international organisation did the USA never join after the war, despite Wilson’s efforts?
29311.e: The US Senate rejected joining because it did not want commitments in Europe. This weakened the organisation from the start.
29311.m: The USA stayed out of the League of Nations.

29312.q: What was the name of the peace programme the US president presented in January 1918?
29312.e: Among other things, the programme called for freedom of the seas, open diplomacy and the self-determination of peoples.
29312.m: The Fourteen Points described a plan for peace.

29313.q: In which country did most American soldiers fight in the First World War?
29313.e: The American troops fought mainly on the Western Front in France. In 1918 they helped stop the last German attacks there.
29313.m: The US soldiers fought mainly in France.

29314.q: How did the USA entering the war affect the course of the war?
a: The Entente got fresh troops and supplies
29314.e: The USA brought soldiers, weapons, food and money to Europe. This gave Great Britain and France a clear advantage over the Central Powers in 1918.
29314.m: With the USA, the Entente got the decisive reinforcement.

29315.q: Which title did Nicholas II hold as the last person in Russia?
29315.e: Nicholas II ruled as Emperor of Russia from 1894. He was the last tsar.
29315.m: Nicholas II was the last tsar of Russia.

29316.q: Against which country did Russia under Nicholas II fight in the First World War from 1914?
29316.e: In the First World War Russia fought together with France and Great Britain against Germany and Austria-Hungary. The heavy defeats greatly weakened the tsar.
29316.m: Under Nicholas II Russia fought against Germany in the First World War.

29317.q: In which revolution did Nicholas II have to abdicate in 1917?
29317.e: After strikes and hunger protests in Petrograd, the tsar lost the support of the army. In March 1917 (February in the old Russian calendar) he abdicated.
29317.m: Nicholas II abdicated after the February Revolution.

29318.q: What happened to Nicholas II and his family in 1918?
a: They were murdered by the Bolsheviks
29318.e: The Bolsheviks held the tsar’s family prisoner in the Urals. In July 1918 they were all shot.
29318.m: The tsar’s family was murdered by the Bolsheviks in 1918.

29319.q: Which wandering preacher had great influence at the court of Nicholas II?
29319.e: Rasputin was seen as a miracle healer and won the trust of the tsarina. Noblemen murdered him in December 1916.
29319.m: Rasputin had great influence on the tsar’s family.

29320.q: Which illness did Alexei, the son of Nicholas II, suffer from?
29320.e: With haemophilia, the blood does not clot properly. Even small injuries were life-threatening for the heir to the throne.
29320.m: The tsar’s son Alexei suffered from haemophilia.

29321.q: What is the name of the day in January 1905 when soldiers in St Petersburg fired on peaceful demonstrators?
29321.e: Workers wanted to hand the tsar a petition. Soldiers fired into the crowd, hundreds died, and trust in Nicholas II fell sharply.
29321.m: Bloody Sunday in 1905 shook people’s trust in the tsar.

29322.q: In which year did the October Revolution take place in Russia?
29322.e: In autumn 1917 revolutionary communists seized power in Petrograd.
29322.m: The October Revolution took place in 1917.

29323.q: Which party seized power in the October Revolution?
29323.e: The radical majority group of the Russian Social Democrats overthrew the Provisional Government. Later it called itself the Communist Party.
29323.m: In the October Revolution the Bolsheviks came to power.

29324.q: Which revolutionary leader travelled back to Russia from exile in Zurich in April 1917?
29324.e: Lenin lived in Switzerland during the war. The German government let him travel through Germany in a sealed train carriage because it wanted unrest in Russia.
29324.m: Lenin returned to Russia from Swiss exile in 1917.

29325.q: Which building in Petrograd did the revolutionaries storm in the October Revolution?
29325.e: The Provisional Government met in the Winter Palace. After it was taken, its ministers were arrested.
29325.m: With the capture of the Winter Palace, the October Revolution triumphed.

29326.q: In which city did the October Revolution begin?
29326.e: At that time St Petersburg was called Petrograd and was the capital of Russia. The Bolsheviks seized power there in autumn 1917.
29326.m: The October Revolution began in Petrograd, today’s St Petersburg.

29327.q: Which army did Leon Trotsky build up after the October Revolution?
29327.e: Trotsky was one of the most important leaders of the revolution. In the civil war he built up the Red Army, which fought against the “Whites”.
29327.m: Leon Trotsky built up the Red Army.

29328.q: With which slogan did the revolutionaries win many supporters in 1917?
29328.e: People were tired of war and hungry, and the farmers wanted their own land. The slogan promised exactly that.
29328.m: “Peace, land and bread” was the revolutionaries’ slogan.

29329.q: Which war followed the October Revolution in Russia?
a: A civil war between Reds and Whites
29329.e: From 1918 to about 1922 the Red Army fought against the “Whites”, the opponents of the revolution. Millions of people died from fighting, hunger and disease.
29329.m: After the October Revolution came the Russian Civil War.

29330.q: Which new organisation was meant to keep peace in the world after the First World War?
29330.e: The League of Nations was created with the peace treaties after the First World War. Its headquarters were in Geneva.
29330.m: The League of Nations was meant to keep the peace after 1919.

29331.q: Which country had to accept the blame for the First World War in the Treaty of Versailles?
29331.e: The treaty made Germany and its allies responsible for the war. That is why Germany had to give up territory and make large payments.
29331.m: In the Treaty of Versailles Germany was blamed for the war.

29332.q: What did Germany have to pay to the victorious powers under the Treaty of Versailles?
a: A fee to join the League of Nations
29332.e: These payments are called reparations. They were meant to make up for the damage of the war, especially in France and Belgium.
29332.m: Germany had to pay reparations after 1919.

29333.q: Which territory did Germany have to return to France in the Treaty of Versailles?
29333.e: Alsace-Lorraine had been German since 1871. With the treaty it went back to France.
29333.m: Alsace-Lorraine went back to France in 1919.

29334.q: What was the strip of land called that separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany after the Treaty of Versailles?
29334.e: Poland was given access to the Baltic Sea. As a result, East Prussia was cut off from the rest of the Reich.
29334.m: The Polish Corridor separated East Prussia from the Reich.

29335.q: What was Germany only allowed to have in small numbers under the Treaty of Versailles?
29335.e: The German army was allowed a maximum of 100,000 soldiers. Tanks, military aircraft and submarines were banned.
29335.m: Germany had to disarm heavily after 1919.

29336.q: What did Germany lose in Africa and the Pacific through the Treaty of Versailles?
29336.e: All German colonies, such as German South West Africa or Cameroon, were handed over to victorious powers as mandated territories.
29336.m: Germany lost all its colonies with the Treaty of Versailles.

29337.q: What term did many Germans use to describe the Treaty of Versailles disapprovingly?
29337.e: Germany was not allowed to take part in the negotiations and had to accept the terms. That is why many spoke of a “dictated peace”, which nationalists later exploited.
29337.m: Many Germans called the Treaty of Versailles a dictated peace.

29338.q: Why is the first German democracy called the “Weimar Republic”?
a: The National Assembly met in Weimar
The first president came from Weimar
The peace treaty was signed in Weimar
29338.e: Because Berlin was unsettled, the National Assembly met in Weimar in 1919 and adopted the constitution there.
29338.m: The Weimar Republic is named after the meeting place of the National Assembly.

29339.q: What did right-wing military men try to do in Berlin in March 1920 with the Kapp Putsch?
29339.e: A putsch is a violent attempt to overthrow the government. Because millions of workers went on strike, the Kapp Putsch collapsed after a few days.
29339.m: A general strike made the Kapp Putsch fail in 1920.

29340.q: Who was the first President of the Weimar Republic?
29340.e: The Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert was elected in 1919 and stayed in office until his death in 1925.
29340.m: Friedrich Ebert was the first President of the Reich.

29341.q: Which right could women in Germany use for the first time in a national election in January 1919?
29341.e: Women’s suffrage was introduced in November 1918. In the election to the National Assembly in January 1919, women could vote and stand for election for the first time; in Switzerland women only got the vote at federal level in 1971.
29341.m: Women in Germany were allowed to vote for the first time in 1919.

29342.q: What did the murder of Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau in 1922 show?
a: The young democracy was in danger
The Kaiser was returning to power
29342.e: Right-wing extremists shot Rathenau in Berlin in June 1922. Political murders like this showed how many enemies the Weimar Republic had.
29342.m: The murder of Walther Rathenau shook the Weimar Republic.

29343.q: Which party was the strongest in every Reichstag election from 1919 to 1930?
29343.e: The Social Democrats won the most votes in every election until 1930. Only in July 1932 were they overtaken by the NSDAP.
29343.m: The SPD was for a long time the strongest party in the Weimar Republic.

29344.q: Which former field marshal became President of the Reich in 1925?
29344.e: During the war Paul von Hindenburg had been head of the Supreme Army Command. He remained President until his death in 1934.
29344.m: Paul von Hindenburg became President of the Reich in 1925.

29345.q: What was the League of Nations, which Germany joined in 1926?
a: An organisation to keep the peace
29345.e: The League of Nations was founded after the First World War and had its headquarters in Geneva. It was meant to settle disputes between states peacefully. In 1933 Germany under Hitler left again.
29345.m: The League of Nations was meant to keep the peace.

29346.q: Which countries occupied the Ruhr in January 1923?
29346.e: Because Germany was behind with its reparations, French and Belgian troops marched into the Ruhr.
29346.m: France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in 1923.

29347.q: How did the German government pay the strikers in the occupied Ruhr in 1923?
a: It printed more and more money
It took out loans in Switzerland
29347.e: The government called for passive resistance and kept paying wages. The money came from the printing press, which greatly fuelled inflation.
29347.m: Printing more and more money drove inflation.

29348.e: With inflation, prices rise, so you can buy less with the same money. With hyperinflation this happens extremely fast.
29348.m: With inflation, money loses its buying power.

29349.q: Why were wages in Germany in 1923 often paid daily or even twice a day?
a: The workers wanted it that way
29349.e: Prices rose so fast that money was worth much less by the evening. That is why people went shopping immediately after being paid.
29349.m: Anyone who got money in 1923 spent it straight away.

29350.q: What did children in Germany sometimes do with the worthless banknotes in 1923?
a: They made kites out of them
They took them to the bank
29350.e: The notes were worth so little that children played with them and made kites. Only with a new currency in November 1923 did money become stable again.
29350.m: In 1923 German paper money was worth almost nothing.

29351.q: Who lost a particularly large amount through the hyperinflation of 1923?
a: Savers with money in the bank
29351.e: Savings became worthless. People with debts, on the other hand, could easily pay them back with worthless money.
29351.m: The hyperinflation wiped out many people’s savings.

29352.q: Roughly how much did a loaf of bread cost in Berlin in November 1923?
29352.e: In November 1923 a loaf cost about 200 billion marks. A year earlier it had cost only a few hundred marks.
29352.m: In 1923 a loaf of bread cost billions of marks.

29353.q: Which fast fashionable dance became famous in the Roaring Twenties?
29353.e: The Charleston came from the USA and became a symbol of the new joy of life in Europe’s dance halls.
29353.m: The Charleston was the fashionable dance of the twenties.

29354.q: Which style of music from the USA shaped the Roaring Twenties?
29354.e: Jazz developed in African American communities, for example in New Orleans. In the 1920s it took over the dance halls of Europe.
29354.m: Jazz was the music of the Roaring Twenties.

29355.q: Which science fiction silent film by Fritz Lang came out in cinemas in 1927?
29355.e: “Metropolis” shows a big city of the future. At the time it was one of the most expensive films in Europe, and today it is part of UNESCO’s Memory of the World.
29355.m: Fritz Lang’s “Metropolis” is a famous film of the twenties.

29356.q: Which school of art and design did Walter Gropius found in Weimar in 1919?
29356.e: The Bauhaus combined art, craft and technology. Its simple, functional shapes still influence architecture and design today.
29356.m: The Bauhaus shaped modern design and modern architecture.

29357.q: Which short women’s hairstyle was considered modern in the 1920s?
29357.e: Many young women had their hair cut short. The bob stood for more freedom and independence.
29357.m: The bob was the modern hairstyle of the twenties.

29358.q: Which country helped Germany out of the crisis with loans in the mid-1920s?
29358.e: American banks lent Germany a lot of money. This helped the economy recover for a few years, until the Great Depression came in 1929.
29358.m: Money from the USA helped Germany in the twenties.

29359.q: Which Swiss town hosted the Winter Olympic Games in 1928?
29359.e: The second Winter Olympic Games took place in the Engadine in 1928. In 1948 the same town was host again.
29359.m: St Moritz hosted the Winter Olympic Games in 1928.

29360.q: At which stock exchange did the stock market crash of 1929 begin?
29360.e: Share prices on the Wall Street stock exchange in New York crashed in October 1929.
29360.m: The stock market crash of 1929 began on Wall Street.

29361.q: What name is used in the USA for the first big day of the crash, 24 October 1929?
29361.e: On this day share prices collapsed and panic broke out. Because the news only reached Europe on the Friday due to the time difference, people there often speak of “Black Friday”.
29361.m: Black Thursday is seen as the start of the stock market crash.

29362.q: Which worldwide crisis followed the stock market crash of 1929?
29362.e: Companies went bust, banks collapsed and world trade shrank sharply. The crisis lasted into the 1930s.
29362.m: The stock market crash led to the Great Depression.

29363.q: What risky thing had many Americans done before the stock market crash of 1929?
29363.e: Many bought shares with borrowed money and hoped prices would rise. When prices fell, they could not pay their debts.
29363.m: Speculating with borrowed money made the crash so severe.

29364.q: How many people were registered as unemployed in Germany at the beginning of 1932?
29364.e: At the height of the crisis, over six million people were registered as unemployed. The hardship strengthened radical parties.
29364.m: In the Great Depression millions of people in Germany were unemployed.

29365.q: What did many people lose in the stock market crash of 1929?
a: The money they had invested in shares
29365.e: Share prices fell sharply within a few days. Anyone who owned shares lost a lot of money. The President of the USA at the time was Herbert Hoover.
29365.m: In the stock market crash of 1929 many people lost their money.

29366.q: What was the name of the programme with which US President Franklin D. Roosevelt fought the crisis from 1933?
29366.e: With the New Deal the state created jobs through building projects, controlled the banks and introduced social security.
29366.m: Roosevelt fought the crisis with the New Deal.

29367.q: After 1929, how did many countries try to protect their economies, which made world trade shrink even more?
29367.e: In 1930 the USA sharply raised many tariffs, and other countries did the same. As a result international trade fell even further.
29367.m: High protective tariffs made the Great Depression worse.

29368.q: Which country did Joseph Stalin come from?
29368.e: Stalin was born in Gori in Georgia in 1878. At that time Georgia belonged to the Russian Empire.

29369.q: What does the adopted name “Stalin” mean?
29369.e: Stalin’s real name was Ioseb Jughashvili. He took the name “Stalin”, from the Russian word for steel, as a revolutionary.

29370.q: Which party post did Stalin take over in 1922 that gave him great power?
29370.e: As General Secretary of the Communist Party he filled important posts with his supporters. This let him later get rid of all his rivals.
29370.m: As General Secretary of the party Stalin expanded his power.

29371.q: What were the labour camps called to which millions of people were deported under Stalin?
29371.e: In the Gulag camp system, prisoners had to do forced labour under harsh conditions. Very many died of hunger, cold and exhaustion.
29371.m: The Gulag was the camp system of the Soviet Union.

29372.q: What were Stalin’s economic plans for building up industry quickly from 1928 called?
29372.e: The state decided what factories had to produce in a certain period. At the same time farming was forcibly combined into collective farms.
29372.m: With Five-Year Plans Stalin pushed industrialisation forward.

29373.q: What do we call Stalin’s wave of persecution from 1936 to 1938 with show trials and mass shootings?
29373.e: Hundreds of thousands were arrested as supposed enemies and shot, among them many party members and officers.
29373.m: In the Great Terror Stalin had hundreds of thousands killed.

29374.q: In which year did Joseph Stalin die?
29374.e: Stalin died near Moscow in March 1953. Afterwards his successor Nikita Khrushchev criticised his crimes.

29375.q: On which day was Adolf Hitler appointed Chancellor of the Reich?
29375.e: On 30 January 1933 the President of the Reich appointed Adolf Hitler Chancellor. This day is seen as the start of Nazi rule in Germany.
29375.m: On 30 January 1933 the Nazi dictatorship began with Hitler’s appointment.

29376.q: What was the name of the secret police created in 1933 that persecuted opponents of the Nazi regime?
29376.e: The Secret State Police, Gestapo for short, was set up in Prussia in 1933. It arrested people without a court ruling and tortured many.
29376.m: The Gestapo was the feared secret police of the Nazis.

29377.q: Which building in Berlin burned in February 1933, which the Nazis used to persecute their opponents?
29377.e: On the night of 27 to 28 February 1933 the Reichstag building burned. On 28 February an emergency decree suspended important basic rights.
29377.m: After the Reichstag fire in 1933 basic rights in Germany were suspended.

29378.q: Which law allowed Hitler’s government to make laws without parliament from March 1933?
29378.e: The Enabling Act was passed by the Reichstag in March 1933. It meant the government could make laws itself, and parliament lost its power.
29378.m: With the Enabling Act the German parliament stripped itself of power in 1933.

29379.q: Which party was the only one present in the Reichstag to vote against the Enabling Act?
29379.e: The SPD members all voted against it; their leader Otto Wels gave a brave speech. The KPD members had already been arrested or had fled.
29379.m: Only the SPD openly voted against the Enabling Act in 1933.

29380.q: What do we call the Nazis bringing clubs, states and trade unions under their control from 1933?
29380.e: With Gleichschaltung, organisations, the media and the states were forced to follow Nazi ideology or were dissolved. That left no independent voices.
29380.m: Through Gleichschaltung the Nazis controlled almost all public life.

29381.q: What did students and Nazis publicly burn in many German cities on 10 May 1933?
29381.e: At the book burning, works by Jewish, left-wing and unwanted authors were thrown into the fire. It showed that free opinion was no longer tolerated.
29381.m: The book burning of 1933 was meant to wipe out unwanted ideas.

29382.q: Which title did Hitler take in 1934 after the death of the President of the Reich?
29382.e: After the President died in August 1934, Hitler combined the offices of President and Chancellor. He now called himself “Führer and Reich Chancellor”.
29382.m: From 1934 Hitler, as “Führer”, held all the power of the state.

29383.q: In which country was Adolf Hitler born in 1889?
29383.e: Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn, which then belonged to Austria-Hungary. Later he moved to Germany.
29383.m: Adolf Hitler originally came from Austria.

29384.q: What is the name of the book in which Hitler set out his world view in the 1920s?
29384.e: Hitler wrote “Mein Kampf” partly while in prison in Landsberg. In it he described his hatred of Jews and his plans for conquest.
29384.m: In “Mein Kampf” Hitler revealed his racial hatred early on.

29385.q: Which career did the young Hitler actually want to follow in Vienna?
29385.e: Hitler applied twice to the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts and was turned down both times. After that he lived in Vienna for some years doing odd jobs.
29385.m: In Vienna the young Hitler failed in his wish to become a painter.

29386.q: How did Adolf Hitler’s life end on 30 April 1945?
a: He took his own life in Berlin
He was killed at the front
29386.e: As the Soviet army captured Berlin, Hitler took his own life in the Führer bunker. In this way he escaped having to answer for his actions in court.
29386.m: In 1945 Hitler escaped all responsibility by taking his own life in the Berlin bunker.

29387.q: What does the abbreviation NSDAP stand for?
29387.e: The NSDAP was Hitler’s party and from 1933 the only party allowed in Germany. Its members were called National Socialists or Nazis.
29387.m: The NSDAP was Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ Party.

29388.q: Which symbol did the NSDAP use on its flag?
29388.e: The party flag showed a black swastika in a white circle on a red background. From 1935 it was even Germany’s national flag.
29388.m: The swastika became the sign of Nazi rule.

29389.q: What was the name of the NSDAP’s fighting force, whose members wore brown shirts?
29389.e: The SA intimidated political opponents with violence, for example in the streets and at meetings. Because of their uniform they were also called “Brownshirts”.
29389.m: The SA was the violent thug squad of the NSDAP.

29390.q: Who was Reich Minister for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda from 1933?
29390.e: Joseph Goebbels controlled the press, radio and film in the interests of the party. Propaganda was used to influence the population.
29390.m: Joseph Goebbels directed the propaganda of the Nazi state.

29391.q: In which city did Jews in the largest ghetto rise up against the SS in 1943?
29391.e: In April 1943 Jewish men and women in the Warsaw Ghetto resisted deportation for weeks. The uprising was brutally crushed.
29391.m: The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising was a sign of Jewish resistance.

29392.q: What was the name of the largest Nazi extermination camp, located in what is now Poland?
29392.e: More than a million people were murdered in Auschwitz-Birkenau, most of them Jews. Today there is a memorial there.
29392.m: Auschwitz has become the symbol of the Holocaust.

29393.q: What did senior Nazi officials discuss at the Wannsee Conference in Berlin on 20 January 1942?
a: The organisation of the murder of the Jews
