30526.e: There are two parallel trails; in one of them, a third individual probably walked in the prints of another. So the tracks come from at least two human ancestors.
30526.m: At Laetoli, at least two human ancestors walked side by side.

30527.q: Which researcher led the excavations in which the Laetoli tracks of human ancestors were discovered in 1978?
30527.e: Mary Leakey's team found animal tracks from 1976 and the tracks of human ancestors in 1978. Jane Goodall and Dian Fossey studied living great apes.
30527.m: Mary Leakey led the work at Laetoli.

30528.q: Which species are the Laetoli footprints usually attributed to?
30528.e: Fossils of Australopithecus afarensis are known from the same time and region. The tracks match the size and foot structure of this species.
30528.m: The Laetoli tracks probably come from Lucy's species.

30529.q: What do the Laetoli footprints show about the feet of the human ancestors?
a: The big toe lay parallel to the others
The big toe stuck out like a thumb
The foot had only four toes
30529.e: The prints show a heel, an arch and a big toe lying close to the others. This matches a foot built for walking on two legs.
30529.m: At Laetoli, the foot already shows a big toe lying alongside the others.

30530.q: What did the study of the tracks at site S in Laetoli, described in 2016, reveal?
a: One individual was unusually tall at about 1.65 metres
The tracks came from children under five
The human ancestors wore leather shoes
The tracks came from four-legged animals
30530.e: From the length of the prints, one individual was estimated to be about 1.65 metres tall. So some of the Laetoli human ancestors were taller than expected.
30530.m: Some of the Laetoli human ancestors were surprisingly tall.

30531.q: What did a 2021 study of the tracks at site A in Laetoli reveal?
a: They come from another two-legged human ancestor
They come from a young bear
They come from an ape walking on four legs
30531.e: The tracks at site A were long thought to be bear tracks. New studies point to a two-legged human ancestor, possibly of a different species from the one at site G.
30531.m: Perhaps two different species of human ancestor walked at Laetoli.

30532.q: In which country is Olduvai Gorge?
30532.e: The gorge lies in northern Tanzania on the edge of the Serengeti. It is part of the East African Rift.

30533.q: Which skull found in Olduvai Gorge became world-famous in 1959?
30533.e: In 1959, Mary Leakey found the skull of a robust human ancestor, now called Paranthropus boisei. Because of its massive molars, it was nicknamed “Nutcracker Man”.
30533.m: Nutcracker Man comes from Olduvai Gorge.

30534.q: Which couple of researchers made Olduvai Gorge world-famous from the 1930s?
30534.e: Louis and Mary Leakey did research at Olduvai for decades. Their finds shaped the picture of early human history in East Africa.
30534.m: Louis and Mary Leakey made Olduvai famous.

30535.q: Apart from fossils, what has been found in large numbers in Olduvai Gorge?
30535.e: The layers of the gorge contain countless pebble tools and flakes. This early tool culture is named Oldowan after the site.
30535.m: Olduvai is rich in early stone tools.

30536.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Site does Olduvai Gorge belong to?
30536.e: Olduvai Gorge lies in the Ngorongoro protected area, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. The area is both natural and cultural heritage.
30536.m: Olduvai Gorge is part of the Ngorongoro World Heritage Site.

30537.q: Why is Olduvai Gorge so valuable for dating fossils?
a: Its walls show layers lying on top of each other that can be dated
It consists of a single block of rock
30537.e: A river has cut the gorge into layers of rock and ash spanning about two million years. Volcanic layers can be dated radiometrically.
30537.m: In Olduvai Gorge, the layers of time lie open like a book.

30538.q: Roughly how long is Olduvai Gorge?
30538.e: The steep-sided gorge is about 48 kilometres long and up to about 90 metres deep. It has a main branch and a side branch.
30538.m: Olduvai Gorge is about 48 kilometres long.

30539.q: Roughly what percentage of their genome do people outside Africa today have from Neanderthals?
30539.e: Genome comparisons show that non-Africans carry about 1 to 2 per cent Neanderthal DNA. This proves gene flow between the two forms of human.
30539.m: Non-Africans carry one to two per cent Neanderthal genome.

30540.q: What does the term “gene flow” mean in genetics?
a: The passing of genes between populations
The loss of genes through mutation
The movement of genes within a cell
Random loss of genes through disease
30540.e: Gene flow means that genetic material passes from one population into another. That is how Neanderthal genes got into the gene pool of Homo sapiens.
30540.m: Gene flow means the exchange of genes between populations.

30541.q: According to recent studies, roughly when did the main mixing between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens take place?
30541.e: Studies of the genomes of ancient and modern humans date the main gene flow to about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. It probably lasted several thousand years.
30541.m: Neanderthals and Sapiens mixed about 47,000 years ago.

30542.q: How were researchers able to prove that Neanderthals and Homo sapiens mixed?
a: By comparing ancient and modern genomes
30542.e: The Neanderthal genome was decoded in 2010. Comparing it with the genome of people today showed shared sections that can only be explained by mixing. Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize for this in 2022.
30542.m: Ancient DNA proves that Neanderthals and Sapiens mixed.

30543.q: In which part of the body do many Neanderthal gene variants that are still common today have an effect?
a: In the lens of the eye
30543.e: Variants of genes for defence receptors often come from Neanderthals. They probably helped modern humans cope with pathogens outside Africa.
30543.m: Neanderthal genes strengthened the immune system of modern humans.

30544.q: What link did Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo find in 2020 for a Neanderthal gene section on chromosome 3?
a: A higher risk of severe Covid-19
30544.e: A section inherited from Neanderthals was linked to a higher risk of severe Covid-19 illness. It is especially common in South Asia.
30544.m: A Neanderthal inheritance affects the risk from Covid-19.

30545.q: How did some Neanderthal genetic material also get into today's African populations?
a: Through people migrating back to Africa
Through Neanderthals who arose in Africa
30545.e: Some modern humans who already carried Neanderthal DNA migrated back to Africa. That is why small amounts of this genetic material are also found in Africans.
30545.m: People migrating back also brought Neanderthal genes to Africa.

30546.q: Which place is the Neanderthal named after?
30546.e: In 1856, bones were found in the Feldhofer Grotto in the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf. This form of human was named after the valley.
30546.m: The Neanderthal is named after the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf.

30547.q: Added up across all people alive today, roughly what share of the Neanderthal genome still survives?
30547.e: Each person carries different Neanderthal sections. Added together, at least about 20 per cent of the Neanderthal genome still survives in humanity today.
30547.m: Spread across all people, a large part of the Neanderthal genome lives on.

30548.q: For what achievement did Svante Pääbo receive the Nobel Prize in 2022?
a: Discoveries about the genomes of extinct forms of human
30548.e: Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the genomes of extinct hominins and on human evolution.
30548.m: Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in 2022 for researching ancient human DNA.

30549.q: Which country does Svante Pääbo come from?
30549.e: Svante Pääbo was born in Stockholm in 1955. He has been doing research in Germany for decades.
30549.m: Svante Pääbo is a Swedish researcher.

30550.q: At which institute did Svante Pääbo become founding director of a department of genetics in 1997?
a: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig
30550.e: Pääbo is a founding director at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. The genomes of the Neanderthals and Denisovans were decoded there.
30550.m: Svante Pääbo does research at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig.

30551.q: Which field of research is Svante Pääbo considered to have played a key part in founding?
30551.e: Palaeogenetics studies genetic material from old bones and sediments. Pääbo developed methods to detect contamination with modern DNA.
30551.m: Svante Pääbo is a pioneer of palaeogenetics.

30552.q: In which material did Svante Pääbo detect ancient human DNA in a paper published in 1985?
a: In a mammoth in the ice
In hair from a bog body
30552.e: As a doctoral student in Uppsala, Pääbo cloned DNA from an Egyptian mummy about 2400 years old. He published the results in “Nature” in 1985.
30552.m: Pääbo's first work with ancient DNA was on an Egyptian mummy.

30553.q: What did Svante Pääbo's team achieve in 1997?
a: Sequencing the mitochondrial DNA of a Neanderthal
30553.e: The team obtained a piece of mitochondrial DNA from the type specimen from the Neander Valley. It was clearly different from the DNA of people today.
30553.m: In 1997, Neanderthal DNA was read for the first time.

30554.q: In which year did Pääbo's team publish the first draft of the Neanderthal genome?
30554.e: In May of that year, the draft of the Neanderthal genome appeared in “Science”. It showed gene flow between Neanderthals and modern humans for the first time.
30554.m: The Neanderthal genome has been known since 2010.

30555.q: What is special about Svante Pääbo's family?
a: His father also received a Nobel Prize in Medicine
30555.e: His father Sune Bergström received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1982. Father and son were therefore honoured in the same category.
30555.m: Svante Pääbo and his father both received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

30556.q: Which particularly big problem in analysing ancient DNA did Pääbo fight with strict laboratory methods?
a: Too much genetic material being present
30556.e: Ancient DNA is badly broken down and only present in traces. Even tiny amounts of DNA from excavators or lab staff can distort the results, so work is done in clean rooms.
30556.m: Ancient DNA must be protected from contamination in clean rooms.

30557.q: In which German state were the Schöningen spears found?
30557.e: The spears come from the open-cast lignite mine near Schöningen in the district of Helmstedt in Lower Saxony. They were excavated from 1994 to 1998.
30557.m: The Schöningen spears come from Lower Saxony.

30558.q: Where were the Schöningen spears discovered?
30558.e: The spears came to light from 1994 to 1998 in the open-cast lignite mine near Schöningen in Lower Saxony. The diggers there uncovered old lake deposits.
30558.m: The Schöningen spears come from an open-cast lignite mine.

30559.q: Which wood are most of the Schöningen spears made of?
30559.e: Most of the spears are made of spruce wood, and one of pine. The makers placed the point in the harder, lower part of the trunk.
30559.m: The Schöningen spears are mostly made of spruce wood.

30560.q: According to a new dating published in 2025, roughly how old are the Schöningen spears?
30560.e: For a long time they were thought to be about 300,000 years old. A 2025 study using improved methods found about 200,000 years.
30560.m: According to new dating, the Schöningen spears are about 200,000 years old.

30561.q: According to the new dating of 2025, which form of human probably made the Schöningen spears?
30561.e: With the younger age of about 200,000 years, the spears fit into the time of early Neanderthals. Before that, Homo heidelbergensis was often named as their maker.
30561.m: The Schöningen spears probably come from early Neanderthals.

30562.q: Which animals were found in large numbers together with the spears at Schöningen?
30562.e: At the site lay the bones of numerous wild horses with cut marks. This points to a planned group hunt on the lake shore.
30562.m: At Schöningen, mainly wild horses were hunted.

30563.q: What do the Schöningen spears prove about the people of that time?
a: They hunted big game deliberately and with planning
They could not yet work wood
They already knew the bow and arrow
30563.e: The carefully carved spears are balanced like modern javelins. They show that people planned ahead and worked together as hunters.
30563.m: The Schöningen spears prove planned big-game hunting.

30564.q: Why did the wooden spears at Schöningen survive for so long?
a: They lay in damp lake deposits low in oxygen
They lay in a dry desert
30564.e: The spears were buried in waterlogged layers of mud at the edge of a former lake. Without oxygen, fungi and bacteria could hardly break down the wood.
30564.m: Lake mud low in oxygen preserved the wooden spears.

30565.q: Why has the original Lascaux cave been closed to visitors since 1963?
a: The visitors' breath and moisture damaged the paintings
The cave was in danger of collapsing
The paintings were taken to a museum
30565.e: The many visitors brought warmth, carbon dioxide and germs into the cave. Algae and mould threatened the paintings, so copies are shown today.
30565.m: Lascaux is closed to protect the paintings.

30566.q: Where do the red, orange and yellow shades at Lascaux come from?
30566.e: Ochre and other iron-containing minerals provided the warm shades. Depending on the iron compound, yellow, orange or red is produced.
30566.m: The warm colours at Lascaux come from iron oxides.

30567.q: What did analyses reveal about how the paints at Lascaux were prepared?
a: They were applied without mixing or heating
They were always burnt with lime
They were boiled with resin to make varnish
They were pressed from plant sap
30567.e: At Lascaux, the mineral pigments were used directly, without mixing or heating them. This sets Lascaux apart from sites where pigments were burnt.
30567.m: At Lascaux, the paints were used without mixing or heating.

30568.q: What is the almost complete replica of the Lascaux cave that opened in Montignac in 2016 called?
30568.e: Lascaux IV at the Centre International d'Art Pariétal reproduces almost the entire cave system. Lascaux II shows only the Hall of the Bulls and the Axial Gallery, and Lascaux III was a touring exhibition.
30568.m: Lascaux IV is the walk-in copy of the whole cave.

30569.q: Which figure in the Hall of the Bulls at Lascaux is called the “Licorne”?
a: A human with a bird's head
A wild horse with a foal
30569.e: At the start of the Hall of the Bulls stands a puzzling animal figure with long, straight horns. Because of its mythical shape, it is called the “Licorne”, meaning unicorn.
30569.m: The “Licorne” is a puzzling mythical animal at Lascaux.

30570.q: Apart from painting, which technique did the artists of Lascaux also use often?
a: They scratched pictures into the rock
They burnt pictures in with fire
30570.e: Besides the paintings, there are about 1500 engravings at Lascaux. Many are so fine that you can hardly see them with the naked eye.
30570.m: There are also many engravings at Lascaux.

30571.q: On which river is the Lascaux cave?
30571.e: Lascaux lies on the left bank of the Vézère, about 2 kilometres south of Montignac. The valley is rich in sites and has been a World Heritage Site since 1979.
30571.m: Lascaux lies in the Vézère valley.

30572.q: How was the Lascaux cave discovered in 1940?
a: Teenagers climbed in through a hole in the woods
Soldiers came across it while building a bunker
A farmer fell in while ploughing
Archaeologists found it with ground radar
30572.e: In September 1940, four teenagers including Marcel Ravidat discovered an opening in the woods near Montignac. They crawled in and found the magnificent animal pictures.
30572.m: Lascaux was discovered by teenagers in 1940.

30573.q: In which area of France is the Chauvet Cave?
a: In the Ardèche valley in southern France
30573.e: The cave lies near Vallon-Pont-d'Arc in the Ardèche. It was discovered in 1994 by three cave explorers and named after Jean-Marie Chauvet.
30573.m: The Chauvet Cave is in the Ardèche.

30574.q: Roughly how old are the oldest paintings in the Chauvet Cave?
30574.e: Dating gives the oldest pictures an age of about 36,000 years. That makes them about twice as old as the pictures at Lascaux.
30574.m: The pictures in the Chauvet Cave are among the oldest cave paintings in the world.

30575.q: Why are the paintings in the Chauvet Cave so well preserved?
a: A rockfall sealed the entrance for thousands of years
The cave lay under a glacier
They were restored in the Middle Ages
30575.e: Over 20,000 years ago, a rockfall buried the original entrance. As a result, the climate in the cave stayed stable and nobody disturbed the pictures.
30575.m: A rockfall sealed the Chauvet Cave for a long time.

30576.q: Which trick did the painters of the Chauvet Cave use to show movement?
a: Sequences of pictures on wooden boards
30576.e: Some animals have doubled legs or heads, which looks like movement. The artists also used bulges in the rock to create a three-dimensional effect.
30576.m: In Chauvet, multiple outlines create the impression of movement.

30577.q: How old is the charcoal from the torch with which a child walked through the Chauvet Cave?
30577.e: The child kept wiping the torch on the wall to make it burn brighter. The charcoal marks were dated to about 26,000 years, so they are younger than the paintings.
30577.m: A child visited the Chauvet Cave long after the first painters.

30578.q: Why did the Chauvet Cave shake the idea of a steady development of cave art?
a: Its very old pictures are already highly developed
Its pictures are younger than those at Lascaux
30578.e: It was assumed that art grew from simple to complex forms. But Chauvet already shows perspective, shading and movement at a very early time.
30578.m: Chauvet proves that art was masterly very early on.

30579.q: Which rare big cat is shown in the Chauvet Cave alongside many cave lions?
30579.e: Among the predators in the Chauvet Cave, besides lions, bears and hyenas, there is also a panther. Such pictures are extremely rare in Ice Age art.
30579.m: A panther is also one of the predators in the Chauvet Cave.

30580.q: Which animals are mainly shown on the famous ceiling of the Altamira cave?
30580.e: The ceiling of the great hall shows mainly bison in red and black. The artists used bulges in the rock so that the animals look almost three-dimensional.
30580.m: Altamira is famous for its bison.

30581.q: Who was the first to notice the ceiling paintings of Altamira in 1879?
a: Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola's little daughter
A shepherd looking for a sheep
30581.e: Sautuola was digging in the cave floor when his daughter María, aged about eight, looked up at the ceiling and spotted animals. The cave itself had been found a few years earlier.
30581.m: A child discovered the ceiling paintings of Altamira.

30582.q: Which cultural stage do the famous ceiling paintings of Altamira belong to?
30582.e: The ceiling paintings with the bison were made around 16,500 to 13,000 BC. This period is the Magdalenian, the last stage of the Upper Palaeolithic.
30582.m: The bison of Altamira date from the Magdalenian.

30583.q: What ended the use of the Altamira cave around 11,000 BC?
a: A volcanic eruption filled it with ash
Ice blocked the way in for ever
30583.e: The cave was used from about 33,600 BC until its entrance collapsed. This kept the pictures protected for a long time.
30583.m: A collapse sealed Altamira for thousands of years.

30584.q: Near which town in Cantabria is the Altamira cave?
30584.e: Altamira lies near Santillana del Mar, about 32 kilometres south-west of Santander. A museum nearby shows a replica.
30584.m: Altamira lies near Santillana del Mar.

30585.q: How was the World Heritage listing of the Altamira cave changed in 2008?
a: It was extended to include other painted caves in northern Spain
It was removed because of damage
It was transferred to the replica
30585.e: Altamira has been a World Heritage Site since 1985. In 2008, further caves with Palaeolithic art in northern Spain were added.
30585.m: Since 2008, the Altamira World Heritage Site has included several caves in northern Spain.

30586.q: Why did Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola not live to see his discovery recognised?
a: He died in 1888, long before his critic took back his doubts
30586.e: Experts suspected Sautuola of forgery, and he died in 1888. Only in 1902 did Cartailhac publicly withdraw his doubts.
30586.m: Sautuola died before he was proved right.

30587.q: In which present-day country was the Venus of Willendorf found?
30587.e: The figure was discovered in 1908 in Willendorf in the Wachau on the Danube. Today it is on display in the Natural History Museum in Vienna.
30587.m: The Venus of Willendorf comes from Austria.

30588.q: What does the fact that the stone of the Venus of Willendorf does not come from the Wachau show?
a: People or materials travelled long distances at that time
The figure was only carved in the Middle Ages
The figure is a modern fake
There were no people in the Wachau
30588.e: According to analyses from 2022, the oolite probably comes from the area around Lake Garda. This proves long journeys or trading links in the Ice Age.
30588.m: The stone of the Venus of Willendorf came from far away.

30589.q: How was the navel of the Venus of Willendorf made?
a: From a natural hollow that was enlarged
30589.e: The carver used a natural hollow in the stone as the navel and deepened it. So he cleverly adapted the figure to the stone.
30589.m: The Venus's navel uses a natural hollow in the stone.

30590.q: With which tool was the Venus of Willendorf probably worked?
30590.e: Fine lines, such as those on the head, were probably engraved with a flint burin. Such tools were found in the same layers.
30590.m: A flint burin shaped the details of the Venus.

30591.q: What do the notches on the thin arms of the Venus of Willendorf probably represent?
30591.e: The arms rest on the chest and have notched lines. They are interpreted as arm jewellery.
30591.m: The Venus of Willendorf probably wears bracelets.

30592.q: Which body parts are missing on the Venus of Willendorf?
30592.e: The figure ends below the knees, and no feet are carved. The face is not shown either.
30592.m: The Venus of Willendorf has no feet.

30593.q: According to newer dating, since when was the Willendorf site inhabited?
30593.e: The site in the Wachau has many layers. The oldest traces go back about 43,500 years, well before the time of the figure.
30593.m: Willendorf was inhabited long before the Venus.

30596.q: Why was the excavation at Hohlenstein-Stadel suddenly stopped in 1939?
a: Because the Second World War broke out
Because the university ran out of money
30596.e: The fragments were recovered on 25 August 1939. Shortly afterwards the war began and the excavation stopped; the pieces were ignored for decades.
30596.m: The start of the war interrupted the excavation of the Lion Man in 1939.

30597.q: What did the new restoration of the Lion Man in 2013 achieve?
a: About 80 more pieces were fitted in
The figure was exposed as a fake
The figure was copied in stone
30597.e: Newly found fragments of the neck and back were fitted in under Nicole Ebinger-Rist. The figure grew from 29.6 to 31.1 centimetres.
30597.m: Since 2013, the Lion Man has been more complete than before.

30598.q: In which valley is the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave?
30598.e: Hohlenstein-Stadel lies in the Lone valley near Asselfingen in the Swabian Jura. Vogelherd and Bockstein are also there.
30598.m: The Lion Man comes from the Lone valley.

30599.q: Why is the Lion Man considered important for the history of ideas?
a: It is one of the oldest images of a mythical creature
It is the oldest tool made of ivory
30599.e: A creature that is part human and part lion does not exist in nature. The figure therefore shows imagination, perhaps myths or rituals.
30599.m: The Lion Man proves early thinking about mythical creatures.

30600.q: In which museum is the Lion Man on display today?
a: In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich
In the British Museum in London
30600.e: The figure has belonged to the city of Ulm since 1956 and is the most important exhibit of the Museum Ulm. It was found in a cave in the nearby Swabian Jura.
30600.m: The Lion Man can be seen in the Museum Ulm.

30601.q: What might the fine notches on the Lion Man's left upper arm show?
30601.e: The parallel grooves are interpreted as showing tattoos or scars. The left ear also has fine cuts.
30601.m: The Lion Man may have body decoration on its arm.

30602.q: How did a flute made of mammoth ivory have to be made?
a: Split lengthways, hollowed out and joined back together
Softened in fire and drilled out
Pressed into a tube from powder
Soaked in water and rolled up
30602.e: Unlike bird bones, ivory is not hollow. The piece had to be split, both halves hollowed out and tightly joined together.
30602.m: An ivory flute required great craftsmanship.

30603.q: What is the famous flute from Hohle Fels made of?
a: The bone of a griffon vulture
30603.e: The flute was made from the wing bone of a griffon vulture and has five finger holes. It was found in the Swabian Jura in 2008.
30603.m: The flute from Hohle Fels is made from a vulture bone.

30604.q: Roughly how old are the oldest flutes from the caves of the Swabian Jura?
30604.e: The flutes from Hohle Fels and Geissenklösterle are about 35,000 to 43,000 years old. They are among the oldest known musical instruments.
30604.m: The oldest flutes in the world are about 40,000 years old.

30605.q: What did replicas of Stone Age flutes, for example by Friedrich Seeberger, show?
a: You can play a variety of tunes on them
They make only a single note
They were really whistles for dogs
They break as soon as you play them
30605.e: Seeberger rebuilt the instruments and tested them. They allow several notes and varied music.
30605.m: Stone Age flutes could play real tunes.

30606.q: What do the flutes from the Swabian Jura prove about cultural history?
a: Music was part of the life of Homo sapiens in Europe early on
Flutes were used only as hunting lures
30606.e: The flutes are among the oldest undisputed musical instruments in the world. They show that music was already part of the culture of the first modern humans in Europe.
30606.m: Music was already part of culture in the Ice Age.

30607.q: Which bone is the disputed find from the Divje Babe cave made of?
a: The thigh bone of a cave bear
30607.e: The 1995 find from Slovenia is the thigh bone of a young cave bear with holes in it. Whether it was made by Neanderthals is disputed.
30607.m: The Divje Babe find is a bear bone.

30608.q: Why were bird bones well suited for making flutes?
a: They are long, thin-walled and hollow inside
They only make sounds under water
30608.e: The wing bones of large birds such as swans or vultures are hollow and sturdy. You only had to drill finger holes, while ivory had to be laboriously split and hollowed out.
30608.m: Hollow bird bones made ideal flute tubes.

30609.q: In which part of the world have strikingly few hand axes been found?
30609.e: The researcher Hallam Movius described how hand axes hardly occur in East and South-East Asia. This is explained by gaps in research, a lack of raw material or tools made of bamboo.
30609.m: Hand axes are rare in East Asia.

30610.q: What is special about the hand axe from Pratteln?
a: It is considered the oldest known tool in Switzerland
It was made by the Romans
It is the largest hand axe in the world
30610.e: The hand axe from Pratteln is over 100,000 years old and is considered the oldest known tool in Switzerland. It is on display in the Museum.BL in Liestal.
30610.m: The hand axe from Pratteln is the oldest tool in Switzerland.

30611.q: What do experts call stone tools like the hand axe that are worked on both faces?
30611.e: With a hand axe, flakes are removed from both sides until a symmetrical shape with an edge all round is created. Such pieces worked on both sides are called bifacial tools or bifaces.
30611.m: A hand axe is a bifacial tool worked on both sides.

30612.q: How did hand axes tend to change over time?
a: They became smaller and more finely worked
30612.e: Early hand axes were often over 20 centimetres long and rough. Later pieces are smaller, more symmetrical and worked with more flakes.
30612.m: Over time, hand axes became smaller and finer.

30613.q: Which site is the Acheulean named after?
30613.e: Saint-Acheul is a suburb of Amiens on the Somme. Many hand axes were found there early on in old river gravels.
30613.m: The Acheulean is named after Saint-Acheul near Amiens.

30614.q: On which continent were the oldest known hand axes found?
30614.e: Hand axes about 1.76 million years old were found at Lake Turkana in Kenya. The technique only reached Europe much later.
30614.m: The oldest hand axes come from Africa.

30615.q: What did hand axes found together with bones of extinct animals in the 19th century prove?
a: That humans have lived on Earth for a very long time
That humans wiped out all these animals
That the tools came from Roman times
30615.e: From 1838, Jacques Boucher de Perthes found hand axes in the Somme next to bones of mammoths and other extinct animals. This showed that humans already lived in the Ice Age.
30615.m: Hand axes next to Ice Age animals proved the great age of humanity.

30616.q: What did the people of the Acheulean probably use hand axes for most of all?
a: As an all-purpose tool for cutting and butchering
As an arrowhead for the bow
30616.e: Wear marks show that hand axes were used for butchering animals, cutting and working wood. The bow and arrow only appeared much later.
30616.m: The hand axe was the all-purpose tool of early humans.

30617.q: Which part of the Old Stone Age does the Acheulean belong to?
30617.e: The Acheulean lasted from almost 2 million to about 150,000 years ago. That puts it in the oldest part of the Old Stone Age.
30617.m: The Acheulean is a culture of the Lower Palaeolithic.

30618.q: What is the Stone Age culture called the Mousterian named after?
a: The site of Le Moustier in France
The monastery of Müstair in the Grisons
The town of Moosburg in Bavaria
30618.e: Le Moustier is a rock shelter in the Vézère valley in the Dordogne. Gabriel de Mortillet named the culture after this site in 1872.
30618.m: The Mousterian is named after Le Moustier.

30619.q: Which flaking technique with a prepared core is typical of the Mousterian?
30619.e: In the Levallois technique, the core is first shaped so that a flake with a planned shape can be struck off. This requires thinking ahead.
30619.m: The Levallois technique shows the Neanderthals' ability to plan.

30620.q: Which type of tool is especially common in the Mousterian?
30620.e: Scrapers in many variants, single, double or curved, dominate Mousterian collections. They were used for working hides and wood, for example.
30620.m: Scrapers are the most common tool in the Mousterian.

30621.q: Which form of human made the Mousterian tools in Europe?
30621.e: In Europe, the Mousterian is the tool culture of the Neanderthals until about 40,000 years ago. In the Middle East, early Homo sapiens also used such tools.
30621.m: The Mousterian is mainly the culture of the Neanderthals.

30622.q: Which older stone tool still appears in a small, heart-shaped form in a late variety of the Mousterian?
30622.e: Small, heart-shaped hand axes are found in a late form of the Mousterian. The hand axe tradition of the Acheulean lived on in it.
30622.m: Hand axes still existed in the Mousterian.

30623.q: What do finds from the Qafzeh and Skhul caves in Israel show?
a: Early Homo sapiens also made Mousterian tools
Neanderthals never lived in the Middle East
The Mousterian only began 20,000 years ago
30623.e: At Qafzeh and Skhul, Mousterian tools are linked with anatomically modern humans. So a culture cannot be rigidly assigned to one form of human.
30623.m: Tool culture and form of human are not always the same thing.

30624.q: Which traces prove that tools were hafted in the Mousterian?
a: Remains of natural adhesives such as bitumen
Imprints of leather straps in clay
30624.e: Remains of bitumen and other glues have been found on stone tools. They were used to fix blades and points to handles or shafts.
30624.m: Neanderthals glued tools to shafts with bitumen.

30625.q: Which rock did the Neanderthals usually make their Mousterian tools from?
30625.e: Flint breaks with a shell-like fracture and forms very sharp edges. Where there was none, people also used quartzite or other hard rocks.
30625.m: Flint was the most important material of the Stone Age.

30626.q: Which place is the Aurignacian named after?
30626.e: The culture is named after a rock shelter near Aurignac in southern France. Gabriel de Mortillet introduced the term in 1867.
30626.m: The Aurignacian is named after Aurignac.

30627.q: Which form of human is considered the bearer of the Aurignacian?
30627.e: Teeth and skulls from sites such as Mladeč and Brassempouy link the Aurignacian with modern humans. Neanderthals were also considered in the past.
30627.m: The Aurignacian is a culture of early modern humans in Europe.

30628.q: Which famous works of art belong to the Aurignacian?
a: The ivory figures of the Swabian Jura
30628.e: Figures such as the Lion Man and the Venus of Hohle Fels are about 40,000 years old and belong to the Aurignacian. Lascaux and Willendorf are younger, and the sky disc dates from the Bronze Age.
30628.m: The ivory figures of the Swabian Jura date from the Aurignacian.

30629.q: Apart from stone, which materials did the people of the Aurignacian often use to make tools and points?
30629.e: In the Aurignacian, bone and antler were worked on a large scale for the first time, for example into projectile points. Metal and glass were not known for a long time to come.
30629.m: In the Aurignacian, bone and antler were made into tools.

30630.q: Roughly how many years ago did the Aurignacian begin in Europe?
30630.e: The Aurignacian began about 40,000 years ago, when modern humans came to Europe. It was later followed by the Gravettian.
30630.m: The Aurignacian began about 40,000 years ago.

30631.q: Which part of prehistory does the Aurignacian belong to?
30631.e: The Aurignacian is the first culture of the Upper Palaeolithic, the later Old Stone Age. Farming and metal only came much later.
30631.m: The Aurignacian belongs to the later Old Stone Age.

30632.q: Roughly how old are the oldest paintings in the Chauvet Cave in southern France?
30632.e: Radiocarbon dates show that the oldest pictures are over 30,000 years old. They are usually assigned to the Aurignacian and are among the oldest cave paintings in the world.
30632.m: The pictures in the Chauvet Cave are over 30,000 years old.

30633.q: What did stone tools found next to bones of Ice Age animals in the rock shelter of Aurignac show in the 19th century?
a: Humans lived at the same time as Ice Age animals
The Romans had a camp there
Dinosaurs still lived in the Ice Age
30633.e: In 1860, Édouard Lartet showed at Aurignac that humans lived at the same time as extinct animals. This was an important step for the young science of prehistory.
30633.m: Aurignac showed that humans lived alongside Ice Age animals.

30634.q: What is the Magdalenian named after?
a: The site of La Madeleine in France
30634.e: The rock shelter of La Madeleine lies in the Vézère valley in the Dordogne. Like many cultures of the Old Stone Age, the Magdalenian is named after a typical site.
30634.m: The Magdalenian is named after La Madeleine.

30635.q: In which period does the Magdalenian fall?
a: At the end of the last Ice Age
30635.e: The Magdalenian lasted from about 20,000 to 14,000 years ago. It is the last great culture of the Old Stone Age in Western Europe.
30635.m: The Magdalenian belongs to the end of the Ice Age.

30636.q: Which barbed hunting weapons made of antler are typical of the Magdalenian?
30636.e: In the Magdalenian, harpoons with barbs on one or both sides were made from reindeer antler. They were also suitable for fishing.
30636.m: Antler harpoons are typical of the Magdalenian.

30637.q: Which works of art are particularly typical of the Magdalenian?
a: Cave paintings such as those at Lascaux and Altamira
30637.e: Many of Europe's most famous cave paintings date from the Magdalenian. There are also decorated tools made of antler and bone.
30637.m: The Magdalenian was a golden age of cave art.

30638.q: Which device did Magdalenian hunters use to throw spears further and with more force?
30638.e: The spear-thrower lengthens the arm like a lever. In the Magdalenian, many spear-throwers made of antler were skilfully decorated with animal figures.
30638.m: With the spear-thrower, Ice Age hunters threw further.

30639.q: On which lake are the Magdalenian sites of Monruz and Hauterive-Champréveyres?
30639.e: Both sites lie near Neuchâtel and were excavated when the A5 motorway was built. They are among the most important Magdalenian camps in Switzerland.
30639.m: Magdalenian hunters camped on Lake Neuchâtel.

30640.q: Which animals were the main prey of Magdalenian hunters?
30640.e: The hunters followed the migrating herds and lay in wait for them at narrow places. That is why this period is also called the Reindeer Age.
30640.m: In the Magdalenian, people mainly hunted reindeer and horses.

30641.q: What changed in Central Europe at the end of the Magdalenian?
a: Forest spread and the reindeer moved north
The glaciers grew as far as the Mediterranean
30641.e: After the Ice Age it became warmer, and forests pushed back the open steppe. The hunters switched to red deer, roe deer and wild boar.
30641.m: The forest brought new animals to hunt.

30642.q: Which later geologist discovered the famous engraved reindeer in the Kesslerloch in 1874?
30642.e: Albert Heim found the piece on 4 January 1874 together with Jakob Messikommer. Heim later became a well-known Alpine geologist.
30642.m: Albert Heim discovered the reindeer from the Kesslerloch.

30643.q: Under what name is the engraved reindeer from the Kesslerloch known today?
30643.e: The engraving used to be called the “Grazing Reindeer”. Today the posture is interpreted as searching, and it is called the “Searching Reindeer”.
30643.m: The “Searching Reindeer” is the best-known work of art from the Kesslerloch.

30644.q: What was strange about the engravings of a fox and a bear from the Kesslerloch?
a: They were fakes copied from a children's book
They were the oldest pictures in the world
30644.e: A worker's nephew carved the pictures in 1875 and passed them off as finds. The researcher Ludwig Lindenschmit realised that they had been copied from a children's book.
30644.m: Fake finds also turned up in the Kesslerloch.

30645.q: Which museum has shown a well-known diorama of the Kesslerloch since 1939?
30645.e: The diorama by Hans Wanner and Juri Richter was considered a milestone in museum design. Today, however, it no longer reflects the state of research.
30645.m: The Museum zu Allerheiligen shows a diorama of the Kesslerloch.

30646.q: Roughly how many years ago did reindeer hunters live in the Kesslerloch?
30646.e: The finds belong to the Magdalenian at the end of the last Ice Age. At that time, reindeer, wild horses and mammoths lived in the area around Thayngen.
30646.m: Reindeer hunters lived in the Kesslerloch about 15,000 years ago.

30647.q: Which finds are completely missing from the Kesslerloch?
30647.e: Although bones of over 50 animal species and many tools were found, there are no human skeletal remains. The people are only known from what they left behind.
30647.m: No human bones were found in the Kesslerloch.

30648.q: Which black material were some pieces of jewellery from the Kesslerloch made of?
30648.e: Jet is a deep black fossil coal that can be polished. In the Old Stone Age it was made into beads and pendants.
30648.m: Jet was a popular stone for jewellery among Ice Age hunters.

30649.q: What did the reindeer hunters probably use the Kesslerloch for?
a: As a store for winter supplies
30649.e: The site in the narrow valley was well suited for hunting migrating herds. It is thought that it was visited mainly in summer.
30649.m: The Kesslerloch was a summer camp of the reindeer hunters.

30650.q: Who lived in the Wildkirchli caves from the 17th to the 19th century?
30650.e: A cave chapel was built in the Wildkirchli in 1621. From 1658, hermits lived there until the last one died in an accident in 1853.
30650.m: Hermits lived in the Wildkirchli for a long time.

30651.q: Bones of which animal were found particularly often during the excavations in the Wildkirchli?
30651.e: Emil Bächler excavated in the Wildkirchli from 1904 and found many cave bear bones. There were also stone tools, which showed that people were already in the Alps in the Old Stone Age.
30651.m: Cave bears once lived in the Wildkirchli.

30652.q: Why was the hermitage in the Wildkirchli given up in 1853?
a: The last hermit fell to his death
A fire destroyed the hermit's cell
30652.e: The hermit Anton Fässler died in an accident in 1853. After that, nobody lived permanently in the caves any more.
30652.m: With the death of Anton Fässler, the Wildkirchli hermitage came to an end.

30653.q: How were the Wildkirchli caves formed?
a: Water dissolved limestone over a long time
A glacier blasted them out of granite
30653.e: The Wildkirchli caves are karst caves in the limestone of the Alpstein. Rainwater containing carbonic acid dissolves the limestone and widens cracks into caves.
30653.m: The Wildkirchli is a karst cave in limestone.

30654.q: Roughly how long is the Wildkirchli cave system altogether?
30654.e: The system consists of several parts with a total length of about 150 metres. One part has two entrances and lies on a hiking trail.
30654.m: The Wildkirchli is about 150 metres long.

30655.q: What has a reconstructed hermit's cell near the Wildkirchli shown since 1972?
a: Paintings of cattle being driven to the alpine pastures
30655.e: Some finds from the excavations are on display in the replica of the hermit's cell. More pieces are shown in the Museum Appenzell.
30655.m: Near the Wildkirchli, you can see finds in a hermit's cell.

30656.q: Who owns the Aescher mountain inn near the Wildkirchli?
30656.e: The inn replaced the hermits' former lodging. It belongs to the Wildkirchli Foundation and is leased out.
30656.m: The Aescher belongs to the Wildkirchli Foundation.

30657.q: From which era do the oldest known spear-throwers come?
a: From the later Old Stone Age
30657.e: The oldest known hook end comes from France and is about 18,000 years old. Most finds belong to the later Magdalenian.
30657.m: The spear-thrower is an invention of the Ice Age.

30658.q: By what factor does the kinetic energy of a spear increase if its speed doubles?
30658.e: Kinetic energy is E equals one half times m times v squared. Double the speed gives 2 squared, so four times the energy.
30658.m: Kinetic energy grows with the square of the speed.

30659.q: Roughly how much kinetic energy does a spear weighing 0.5 kg have at 150 km/h?
30659.e: 150 km/h is 150 ÷ 3.6, which is about 41.7 m/s. E is 0.5 times 0.5 kg times (41.7 m/s) squared, which gives about 434 joules.
30659.m: To work out kinetic energy, first convert km/h into m/s.

30660.q: How fast does the spear tip become if, at the same angular speed, the throwing radius doubles from 0.7 m to 1.4 m?
30660.e: For the speed along the path, v equals angular speed times radius. If the radius doubles, v doubles too.
30660.m: A longer lever makes the spear faster.

30661.q: Which material are most surviving hook ends of spear-throwers made of?
30661.e: Ice Age hunters often carved the hook ends from antler and decorated them with animal figures such as ibex or horses. Metal was not known at that time.
30661.m: Hook ends of spear-throwers are mostly made of antler.

30662.q: Why is it thought that many spear-throwers were made entirely of wood?
a: Because only a few hook ends have survived
Because there was no antler in the Ice Age
Because pictures show only wooden tools
Because wood is harder than bone
30662.e: Only about 120 hook ends made of antler are known, and they are widely scattered. Wood rots in the ground, which is why most of the tools are missing.
30662.m: Many spear-throwers have rotted away because they were made of wood.

30663.q: According to reconstructions, roughly how long were the spears thrown with spear-throwers?
30663.e: Reconstructions give spears about 2.10 to 2.30 metres long. Feathers at the end may have stabilised their flight.
30663.m: Spear-thrower spears were just over two metres long.

30664.q: Up to what distance did people usually hunt with the spear-thrower?
30664.e: In competitions, throws reach up to 140 metres. For accurate hunting, however, the distances were usually under 30 metres.
30664.m: The spear-thrower was most effective at short hunting distances.

30665.q: Which area is known as the Fertile Crescent?
a: The arc from the Levant to Mesopotamia
The Nile valley as far as Sudan
30665.e: The Fertile Crescent is an arc-shaped belt of fertile land from the Levant across south-eastern Anatolia to Mesopotamia. Farming and livestock keeping began here.
30665.m: The Fertile Crescent stretches from the Levant to Mesopotamia.

30666.q: Which cereals were among the first crops in the Fertile Crescent?
30666.e: Emmer, einkorn and barley, together with lentils, peas, chickpeas, bitter vetch and flax, are among the founder crops. Maize and potatoes come from the Americas, rice from Asia.
30666.m: Emmer, einkorn and barley were the first cereals of the Near East.

30667.q: Which plant is one of the founder crops of the Fertile Crescent?
30667.e: Flax (linseed) was used early on for fibres and oil and is one of the eight founder crops. Oats and rye only became important as crops later, and millet comes mainly from East Asia and Africa.
30667.m: Flax is one of the oldest crops of the Near East.

30668.q: What was still missing in the earliest Neolithic of the Near East, even though people already farmed?
30668.e: Experts call it the Pre-Pottery Neolithic. People grew grain and lived in houses, but vessels made of fired clay only came later.
30668.m: The earliest Neolithic had farming but no pottery yet.

30669.q: Which climate change is often discussed as one trigger for the beginning of farming in the Near East?
a: A sudden return to cold at the end of the Ice Age
A heatwave in the Middle Ages
30669.e: The Younger Dryas (about 10,900 to 9700 BC) brought a sudden return to cold and dry conditions. Scarcer wild plants may have encouraged the growing of grain.
30669.m: A cold spell at the end of the Ice Age may have encouraged farming.

30670.q: Which animal was already domesticated in the Zagros Mountains in present-day Iran around 8000 BC?
30670.e: Bone finds from Ganj Dareh prove that goats were kept there around 8000 BC. Horses were only domesticated thousands of years later on the steppes.
30670.m: Goats were domesticated early in the Zagros Mountains.

30671.q: Why can the Neolithic site of Abu Hureyra in Syria no longer be studied today?
a: It was flooded by a reservoir
A city was built over it
It was buried by moving dunes
It sank into the sea in an earthquake
30671.e: Abu Hureyra was investigated in a rescue excavation before the Tabqa Dam was built on the Euphrates. Today the site lies under Lake Assad.
30671.m: Abu Hureyra now lies under the waters of Lake Assad.

30672.q: Where did the researcher Robert Braidwood think farming began?
a: On the slopes of the mountains around Mesopotamia
In the river oases of Egypt
In the forests of Central Europe
30672.e: Braidwood excavated at Jarmo in northern Iraq from 1948. He thought that farming had begun on the mountain slopes, where wild cereals and wild animals occurred naturally.
30672.m: Braidwood looked for the beginnings of farming on the mountain slopes.

30673.q: What do the arms and hands carved on some pillars at Göbekli Tepe suggest?
a: The pillars served as boundary stones
30673.e: Arms, hands, belts and loincloths on the central pillars make them look like highly stylised figures. They are interpreted as humans, ancestors or supernatural beings.
30673.m: Some pillars at Göbekli Tepe are stylised figures with arms and hands.

30674.q: Roughly how old are the oldest stone circles at Göbekli Tepe?
30674.e: The structures were built from about 9500 BC, thousands of years before Stonehenge and the pyramids. Their builders did not yet know pottery.
30674.m: Göbekli Tepe is about 11,000 years old.

30675.q: In which country is Göbekli Tepe, often called the oldest temple in the world?
30675.e: Göbekli Tepe lies in south-eastern Turkey near Şanlıurfa, close to the Syrian border. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018.
30675.m: Göbekli Tepe is in south-eastern Turkey.

30676.q: What is particularly surprising about Göbekli Tepe for the history of humanity?
a: Hunter-gatherers already built huge stone structures
It was built by the Romans
It is a natural rock formation
The oldest written characters were found there
30676.e: It was long believed that only settled farmers could build monuments. But Göbekli Tepe was built at a time when farming was only just beginning.
30676.m: Göbekli Tepe shows that monuments were built before farming was fully developed.

30677.q: What do newer studies at Göbekli Tepe show, in contrast to the original interpretation as a pure sanctuary?
a: There were also houses and water stores
It was a Roman army camp
The site was an obsidian mine
The pillars only date from the Middle Ages
30677.e: Klaus Schmidt saw Göbekli Tepe mainly as a place of worship without a settlement. Later excavations found houses, cisterns and traces of intensive grain processing.
30677.m: Göbekli Tepe was probably also a place to live and not just a sanctuary.

30679.q: Which stone figure from the time of Göbekli Tepe is considered one of the oldest life-size human statues?
30679.e: The Urfa Man is about 1.9 metres tall and is dated to around 9000 BC. It was found during building work in Şanlıurfa in south-eastern Turkey.
30679.m: The Urfa Man is one of the oldest life-size statues.

30680.q: Which animals are often shown in relief on the pillars of Göbekli Tepe?
a: Wild animals such as foxes, snakes and vultures
Farm animals such as cows and sheep
Sea creatures such as whales and dolphins
Mythical creatures such as dragons and griffins
30680.e: The reliefs mainly show dangerous wild animals such as foxes, snakes, wild boar and vultures. There were hardly any farm animals at that time, because keeping livestock was only just beginning.
30680.m: Göbekli Tepe shows wild animals, not farm animals.

30681.q: What does a famous wall painting at Çatalhöyük probably show?
30681.e: The painting shows houses with a mountain with two peaks above them. Many interpret it as the volcano Hasan Dağı and thus as one of the oldest pictures of a landscape.
30681.m: A wall painting at Çatalhöyük probably shows a volcano.

30682.q: In which present-day country is the Neolithic settlement of Çatalhöyük?
30682.e: Çatalhöyük lies in central Anatolia near Konya. It is one of the largest settlements of the New Stone Age and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
30682.m: Çatalhöyük is in Anatolia in Turkey.

30683.q: What is the West Mound of Çatalhöyük?
a: A later settlement of the Copper Age
30683.e: Next to the Neolithic East Mound lies the smaller West Mound. It was settled from about 5600 BC in the early Copper Age, when the East Mound was abandoned.
30683.m: The West Mound of Çatalhöyük is younger than the East Mound.

30684.q: According to current knowledge, what is strikingly missing at Çatalhöyük?
a: Palaces and other large public buildings
30684.e: The houses are very similar in size and furnishings. That is why the society is thought to have been fairly equal, without a clear ruling class.
30684.m: There were no palaces at Çatalhöyük, and the houses were of similar size.

30685.q: How did the high settlement mound of Çatalhöyük come about?
a: Houses were built again and again on the remains of older houses
It was piled up as a defensive wall
A volcano covered the settlement with ash
30685.e: Old houses were filled in and new ones built on top, often with the same floor plan. Over more than a thousand years, this created a mound about 20 metres high.
30685.m: At Çatalhöyük people built house upon house, and so the mound grew.

30686.q: How have newer studies changed the estimates of Çatalhöyük's population?
a: They are much lower than the older estimates
They are ten times higher than the older estimates
They show that nobody ever lived there permanently
They show that the population grew to over 100,000 people
30686.e: Older estimates assumed 5000 to 7000 inhabitants. Newer studies reckon with more like a few hundred people in an average year of the middle phase.
30686.m: Çatalhöyük probably had fewer inhabitants than was once thought.

30687.q: How were the inside walls of the houses at Çatalhöyük looked after?
a: They were coated again and again with thin layers of white plaster
They were covered with wooden boards
They were knocked down every year and rebuilt in stone
They were lined with animal skins
30687.e: Some walls have dozens to over a hundred fine layers of plaster. Older paintings survived underneath them and are uncovered layer by layer during excavation.
30687.m: At Çatalhöyük, house walls were plastered again and again.

30688.q: How much of the height of the Neolithic tower of Jericho still survives?
30688.e: The massive stone tower is about 8.5 metres high and was built around 8000 BC. It is considered one of the oldest stone buildings in the world.
30688.m: The tower of Jericho is about 8.5 metres high.

30689.q: Why did early Jericho grow up in exactly this place?
a: Because of a plentiful spring in the oasis
Because of a harbour on the Mediterranean
Because of a volcano that gave warmth
30689.e: The spring of Ain es-Sultan still provides water today. In the dry Jordan Valley it made farming and a permanent settlement possible.
30689.m: A spring made Jericho an early oasis.

30690.q: How did the people of Neolithic Jericho decorate some skulls of the dead?
a: They modelled faces on them in plaster
They built them into the town wall
They carved cups out of them
30690.e: On some skulls they modelled facial features in plaster and set in shells as eyes. This is interpreted as a way of honouring ancestors.
30690.m: In Jericho, skulls were made into images of ancestors.

30691.q: Which Bible story is Jericho known for to many people?
a: The walls falling down at the sound of trumpets
30691.e: According to the Bible, the walls of Jericho fell when the Israelites under Joshua blew trumpets. However, archaeologists have found no matching town wall from that time.
30691.m: The walls of Jericho are known from the Bible.

30692.q: In which present-day area is ancient Jericho?
30692.e: Tell es-Sultan lies near the town of Jericho in the West Bank, close to the River Jordan. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.
30692.m: Ancient Jericho is in the West Bank.

30693.q: Which interpretation of the tower of Jericho did researchers suggest in 2011?
a: It was linked to the sunset on the summer solstice
It was a lighthouse for ships
It was a Roman grain store
30693.e: On the longest day, the shadow of a nearby mountain falls exactly on the tower at sunset. The researchers therefore saw it as a symbolic building that brought people together for shared work.
30693.m: The tower of Jericho may have been linked to the summer solstice.

30694.q: Early Jericho belongs to the “Pre-Pottery Neolithic”. What does that mean?
a: New Stone Age before the invention of pottery
Old Stone Age before the use of fire
The time before people settled down
30694.e: The people of Jericho were already settled and farmed, but did not yet know vessels made of fired clay. At first they lived in round houses made of mud bricks.
30694.m: In the Pre-Pottery Neolithic there were villages, but no pottery yet.

30695.q: What set of chromosomes does emmer have?
30695.e: Emmer (Triticum dicoccum) came from a cross between two wild grasses and has four sets of chromosomes. Only bread wheat is hexaploid.

a: Through a natural cross between two wild grasses
Through genetic engineering in the 20th century
Through crossing barley and oats in the Middle Ages
30696.e: Emmer arose in the Near East from a natural cross between wild Urartu wheat and a goatgrass. That is why it has four sets of chromosomes.
30696.m: Emmer came from two wild grasses.

30697.q: Under which name is emmer still grown and eaten in Italy today?
30697.e: In Italy, emmer is called “farro” or, more precisely, “farro medio”. Orzo is barley and grano saraceno is buckwheat.
30697.m: In Italy, emmer is called farro.

30698.q: What set of chromosomes does einkorn have?
30698.e: Einkorn (Triticum monococcum) has only two sets of chromosomes. This makes it the simplest cultivated type of wheat.

30699.q: Where does the wild form of einkorn still grow today?
30699.e: Wild einkorn (Triticum boeoticum) still grows in the Near East today. That is also where einkorn was first cultivated.
30699.m: Wild einkorn grows in the Near East.

30700.q: Why is flour made from einkorn noticeably yellowish?
a: It contains a lot of carotenoids such as lutein
It contains a lot of iron
30700.e: Einkorn contains far more carotenoids, especially lutein, than modern wheat. These pigments give the flour its yellow colour.
30700.m: Einkorn flour is yellow because of carotenoids.

30701.q: To roughly which period is the Linear Pottery culture dated?
30701.e: The Linear Pottery culture was the first farming culture spread widely across Central Europe. It lasted from about 5500 to 4900 BC.
30701.m: The Linear Pottery culture brought farming to Central Europe around 5500 BC.

30702.q: Which type of house is typical of the Linear Pottery culture?
a: The round house made of mud bricks
30702.e: Linear Pottery longhouses were often 20 to over 30 metres long and stood on five rows of wooden posts. They had room for people, supplies and perhaps animals.
30702.m: The Linear Pottery people lived in long post-built houses.

30703.q: What were the polished stone axes of the Linear Pottery people mainly used for?
30703.e: The Linear Pottery people needed a lot of wood for their longhouses and cleared forest for fields. For this they used polished stone axes, called shoe-last adzes because of their shape.
30703.m: The Linear Pottery people worked wood with polished stone axes.

30704.q: What does the mass grave at Talheim from the time of the Linear Pottery culture prove?
a: Deadly violence between groups of people
30704.e: At Talheim near Heilbronn, 34 dead people with wounds from blows lay in a pit. The find shows that there were deadly conflicts around 5000 BC.
30704.m: The Talheim mass grave is evidence of violence at the end of the Linear Pottery culture.

30705.q: From which area did the Linear Pottery culture spread into Central Europe?
30705.e: The Linear Pottery culture arose in Transdanubia from forerunners such as the Starčevo-Körös culture. From there it spread quickly westwards as far as the Paris Basin.
30705.m: The Linear Pottery culture comes from western Hungary.

30706.q: Why have wooden wells of the Linear Pottery people survived for over 7000 years?
a: The wood lay in groundwater without air
The wood was coated with tar
The wood has turned to stone over time
The wood was covered with bronze fittings
30706.e: Groundwater lacks oxygen, so bacteria and fungi can hardly break down the wood. This is how the well at Erkelenz-Kückhoven from around 5100 BC survived, for example.
30706.m: Without oxygen, wood in groundwater survives for thousands of years.

30707.q: What material was the prized jewellery of the Linear Pottery people made of that came from the Mediterranean?
30707.e: Shells of the thorny oyster Spondylus were traded in from the Aegean or the Adriatic. They were made into bracelets and beads.
30707.m: Spondylus jewellery shows the long-distance trade of the Linear Pottery people.

30708.q: What are researchers puzzling over with the cut-up human bones from Herxheim from the Linear Pottery period?
a: Whether it was cannibalism or a cult of the dead
Whether they were victims of a volcanic eruption
Whether they are bones of Roman soldiers
Whether the bones came from Neanderthals
30708.e: At Herxheim in the Palatinate, bones of several hundred people with cut and break marks were found. Whether this was cannibalism or a cult of the dead is debated.
30708.m: The finds from Herxheim still puzzle researchers today.

30709.e: The word comes from Greek: “mégas” means large and “líthos” means stone. Megalithic structures such as dolmens or menhirs are made of huge blocks of stone.

30710.q: On which island are the temples of Ġgantija, among the oldest free-standing stone buildings in the world?
30710.e: The temples of Ġgantija on the Maltese island of Gozo were built around 3600 BC. They are part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Megalithic Temples of Malta.
30710.m: The temples of Ġgantija are on Gozo.

30712.q: What is the large Neolithic stone circle on the Orkney Islands called?
30712.e: The Ring of Brodgar originally had about 60 stones and is part of the World Heritage Site “Heart of Neolithic Orkney”. Callanish is in the Outer Hebrides, and Castlerigg and Avebury are in England.
30712.m: The Ring of Brodgar is the great stone circle of Orkney.

30713.q: What is the underground Neolithic burial site on Malta that was cut into the rock called?
30713.e: The Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum is a structure on several levels carved out of the rock. The remains of thousands of people were found in it.
30713.m: The Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum is an underground rock tomb on Malta.

30714.q: Which culture built most of the megalithic tombs in northern Germany and southern Scandinavia?
30714.e: The Funnelbeaker culture built thousands of dolmens and passage graves, mainly between about 3500 and 2800 BC. It is named after the funnel-shaped rims of its pots.
30714.m: The Funnelbeaker people built most of the megalithic tombs in the north.

30715.q: In which village in the canton of Bern was a Neolithic dolmen with many burials discovered in 2011?
30715.e: The Oberbipp dolmen was built in the second half of the 4th millennium BC and used for a long time as a collective grave. Bones of about 30 people were found in it.
30715.m: There is a Neolithic dolmen in Oberbipp in the canton of Bern.

30716.q: According to a 2019 study, from which region did Europe's megalithic buildings probably spread?
30716.e: An analysis of over 2000 radiocarbon dates found the oldest megalithic tombs in north-western France around 4500 BC. From there the idea probably spread by sea.
30716.m: The megalithic idea probably spread by sea from north-western France.

30717.q: What did the first building phase of Stonehenge around 3000 BC begin with?
30717.e: First came a round earthwork ditch with a bank and the Aubrey Holes. The great sarsen stones were only put up around 2500 BC.
30717.m: Stonehenge began as a round ditch with a bank.

30718.q: What is the large Neolithic site near Stonehenge where the builders probably feasted and lived called?
30718.e: Durrington Walls lies about three kilometres north-east of Stonehenge. Remains of many houses and pig bones from great feasts were found there.
30718.m: The builders of Stonehenge probably lived at Durrington Walls.

30720.q: What is the path lined with ditches that links Stonehenge with the River Avon called?
30720.e: The Avenue runs about three kilometres from Stonehenge to the Avon. Its first section follows the axis of the solstices.
30720.m: The Avenue links Stonehenge with the River Avon.

30721.q: Who are the Aubrey Holes at Stonehenge named after?
30721.e: John Aubrey was the first to describe the pits in the 17th century. The 56 holes probably originally held bluestones.
30721.m: The Aubrey Holes are named after John Aubrey.

30722.q: What is the single large stone outside the circle of Stonehenge, above which the sun rises at the summer solstice, called?
30722.e: The Heel Stone stands on the Avenue north-east of the circle. Seen from the centre, the sun rises close to it on Midsummer's Day.
30722.m: The Heel Stone marks the direction of sunrise at the summer solstice.

30723.q: What is Stonehenge proven to have also been used for in its early phase?
a: As a burial site for cremations
As a workshop for casting bronze
30723.e: In the Aubrey Holes and the ditch, burnt bones of many people were found, from 63 people in a re-examination in 2013 alone. So early on, Stonehenge was also an important cemetery.
30723.m: Early on, Stonehenge was also a burial site.

30724.q: In which English county is Stonehenge?
30724.e: Stonehenge lies on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire in southern England. The stone circle of Avebury is in the same county.
30724.m: Stonehenge is in the county of Wiltshire.

30725.q: In which French region are the stone rows of Carnac?
30725.e: Carnac lies on the south coast of Brittany. The three large fields are called Le Ménec, Kermario and Kerlescan.
30725.m: The stone rows of Carnac are in Brittany.

30726.q: To which period are the stone rows of Carnac usually dated?
30726.e: The stone rows were put up in the New Stone Age. Exact dating is difficult, but it usually falls in the 5th and 4th millennia BC.
30726.m: The stone rows of Carnac date from the New Stone Age.

30727.q: What is the large Neolithic burial mound in the village of Carnac called?
30727.e: The Tumulus Saint-Michel is a huge mound with burial chambers, with a chapel standing on top of it today. Silbury Hill, Knowth and Maeshowe are in the British Isles.
30727.m: The Tumulus Saint-Michel is a large burial mound in Carnac.

30728.q: What does a Breton legend say about how the stone rows of Carnac came about?
a: Saint Cornelius turned Roman soldiers into stone
Giants played skittles with the stones
A dragon laid the stones as eggs
The Devil used them to build a bridge into the sea
30728.e: According to the legend, Pope Cornelius fled from Roman soldiers and turned them into stone. He is the patron saint of Carnac.
30728.m: According to legend, the stones of Carnac are soldiers turned to stone.

30729.q: What stands at the ends of the stone rows of Le Ménec?
a: An oval of stones, called a cromlech
30729.e: The rows of Le Ménec end in the west and east in an oval stone enclosure. The stones also get bigger towards the western end.
30729.m: The rows of Le Ménec end in a cromlech.

30730.q: What are the single standing stones that make up the rows of Carnac called?
30730.e: A menhir is a single standing stone. A dolmen, by contrast, is a tomb made of supporting stones with a capstone.
30730.m: The stone rows of Carnac are made of menhirs.

30731.q: Why have the large stone rows of Carnac mostly been fenced off since 1991?
a: To protect them from erosion caused by visitors
Because the menhirs might fall over
Because it is a military area
Because of ongoing searches for gold
30731.e: Hundreds of thousands of visitors had trampled the ground and put the stones at risk. Since then, the fields may only be entered on a limited basis, for example in winter or on a guided tour.
30731.m: Fences protect the stone rows of Carnac from wear and tear.

30732.q: What does the Museum of Prehistory in Carnac mainly show?
a: Finds from the region's New Stone Age
Ships from the Second World War
30732.e: The museum grew out of the collection of the researcher James Miln in 1881. It shows stone axes, jewellery and pottery from the burial sites around Carnac.
30732.m: The Carnac museum shows the New Stone Age of Brittany.

30733.q: Which plant family does rice belong to?
30733.e: Like wheat, barley and maize, rice is a grass. Asian rice descends from a wild rice grass.
30733.m: Rice is a cereal from the grass family.

30734.q: On which river in China did early wet rice farming develop?
30734.e: Many early rice finds were made in the wet lowlands of the lower Yangtze, for example at Hemudu. On the Yellow River in the north, on the other hand, people mainly grew millet.
30734.m: Rice was grown early on the Yangtze.

30735.q: What kind of houses did the early rice farmers of Hemudu live in, in the wet lowlands?
30735.e: At Hemudu, wooden houses stood on stilts above the wet ground. In the waterlogged soil, wood and rice grains were well preserved.
30735.m: At Hemudu, people lived in stilt houses.

30736.q: Which woodworking technique is already proven at Hemudu around 5000 BC?
30736.e: Beams with tenons and mortises were found in the stilt houses of Hemudu. Iron was not yet known at that time.
30736.m: At Hemudu, beams were already joined with tenons.

30737.q: Why did early rice cultures in China such as Liangzhu build large dams and canals?
a: For irrigation and protection from floods
To fend off armies on horseback
30737.e: The Liangzhu culture (about 3300 to 2300 BC) controlled the water for its rice fields with dams and canals. Its city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019.
30737.m: Wet rice farming needs well-controlled water.

30738.q: According to current knowledge, in which present-day country was rice first domesticated?
30738.e: Archaeological and genetic studies show that rice was first bred in southern China. From there it spread to South and East Asia.
30738.m: Rice was first domesticated in China.

30739.q: How did wet rice farming come to Japan?
a: From the Asian mainland, for example via Korea
It arose in Japan completely independently
30739.e: In the 1st millennium BC, immigrants from the mainland brought wet rice farming and metalworking to Japan. This marked the start of the Yayoi period.
30739.m: Wet rice farming came to Japan from the mainland.

30740.q: Roughly how old are the oldest traces of rice use in China?
30740.e: Rice husks about 10,000 years old were found in pottery of the Shangshan culture on the Yangtze. They are among the oldest evidence of rice use.
30740.m: Rice has been used in China for about 10,000 years.

30741.q: Which wild grass is considered the ancestor of maize?
30741.e: Maize descends from teosinte (Zea mays ssp. parviglumis). It hardly looks like modern maize and has only small, hard ears.

30742.q: In which present-day country was maize originally bred from a wild grass?
30742.e: Genetic studies show that maize was bred in south-western Mexico. From there it spread throughout the Americas.

30743.q: According to genetic estimates, roughly how many years ago did the domestication of maize begin?
30743.e: Genetic analyses date the beginning to about 9000 years ago. Starch grains from the Balsas valley give similar dates.
30743.m: Maize has been grown for about 9000 years.

30744.q: How do the oldest maize cobs found differ from today's?
a: They were only a few centimetres long
30744.e: The cobs from Guilá Naquitz cave in Mexico, about 6000 years old, are barely as long as a finger. Through thousands of years of selection, the cobs became bigger and bigger.
30744.m: Through breeding, maize cobs became bigger and bigger.

30745.q: Which plants, together with maize, make up the “Three Sisters” of Indigenous farming in the Americas?
30745.e: Maize gives the beans something to climb, beans fix nitrogen, and squash leaves shade the ground. This mixed planting is also known as milpa.
30745.m: Maize, beans and squash are the Three Sisters.

30746.q: Which maize dish is traditionally made from maize that has first been cooked with lime?
30746.e: Cooking with lime, called nixtamalisation, makes the vitamin niacin available to the body and the dough easy to shape. Without this process, a one-sided diet of maize can lead to the deficiency disease pellagra.
30746.m: For tortillas, maize is cooked with lime.

a: At the end of the 15th century
30747.e: Christopher Columbus brought maize back to Spain from his voyages. From there it spread through Europe in the 16th century.
30747.m: Maize only came to Europe with Columbus.

30748.q: How does the wild plant teosinte differ from modern maize?
a: It is heavily branched and has tiny, hard ears
It has bigger cobs than maize
30748.e: Teosinte branches a lot and forms ears with a few rock-hard grains. A few genetic changes turned it into the unbranched maize plant with a large cob.
30748.m: Maize was bred from the bushy teosinte.

30749.q: To roughly which period is the Bell Beaker culture dated?
30749.e: The Bell Beaker culture belongs to the end of the New Stone Age and the Copper Age. In Central Europe it was widespread mainly from about 2600 to 2200 BC.
30749.m: The Bell Beaker culture flourished around 2600 to 2200 BC.

30750.q: According to the majority view today, in which area did the bell beakers originate?
30750.e: The oldest bell beakers probably come from Portugal, for example from the area around the mouth of the Tagus. From there the beaker shape spread across Europe.
30750.m: The bell beakers probably come from the Iberian Peninsula.

30751.q: Which type of grave goods found with men of the Bell Beaker culture points to archery?
30751.e: Stone wrist guards protected the wrist from the string as it sprang back. They are often found together with arrowheads and copper daggers.
30751.m: Wrist guards point to archers of the Bell Beaker culture.

30752.q: According to isotope analyses, where did the “Amesbury Archer”, buried near Stonehenge, spend his childhood?
30752.e: Isotopes in his tooth enamel show that he grew up in the Alpine region, for example in today's Switzerland, Austria or southern Germany. His grave from around 2300 BC was the richest of its time in Great Britain.
30752.m: The Amesbury Archer grew up in the Alpine region.

30753.q: Which necropolis in Valais contains dolmens and human-shaped stelae that were reused in the Bell Beaker period?
30753.e: Dolmens and decorated stelae were found in the Petit-Chasseur necropolis in Sion. The Bell Beaker people continued to use the graves and reworked stelae.
30753.m: The Petit-Chasseur necropolis in Sion is evidence of the Bell Beaker period in Valais.

30754.q: What did DNA analyses from 2018 show about the Bell Beaker period in Britain?
a: A large-scale replacement of the population
30754.e: With the bell beakers, people with steppe ancestry in their genome came to Britain. Within a few centuries, most of the older Neolithic ancestry was replaced.
30754.m: With the Bell Beaker culture, Britain's population changed greatly.

30755.q: Which buttons are typical of graves of the Bell Beaker culture?
30755.e: The buttons made of bone, amber or jet have a V-shaped hole drilled in the back. This allowed them to be sewn onto clothing.
30755.m: Buttons with V-shaped perforations are typical of the Bell Beaker culture.

30756.q: Which metals spread across large parts of Europe with the Bell Beaker culture?
30756.e: Copper daggers and early gold jewellery are found in Bell Beaker graves. Iron only appeared more than a thousand years later.
30756.m: The Bell Beaker people knew copper and gold.

30757.q: To roughly which period is the Corded Ware culture dated?
30757.e: Corded Ware is a culture of the end of the New Stone Age. It was widespread from about 2800 to 2200 BC.
30757.m: Corded Ware belongs to the period around 2800 to 2200 BC.

30758.q: Under which other name is the Corded Ware culture known because of typical grave goods?
30758.e: Men's graves often contained carefully polished stone axes with a shaft hole. That is why it is also called the Battle Axe culture.
30758.m: Because of its stone axes, Corded Ware is also called the Battle Axe culture.

30759.q: In which body position were the dead of the Corded Ware culture usually buried?
a: On their side with legs drawn up
30759.e: The dead lay on their side in a crouched position with bent legs. Men and women were usually laid on opposite sides, like mirror images.
30759.m: The Corded Ware people buried their dead in a crouched position.

30760.q: With which steppe culture do DNA analyses show a close genetic relationship to the Corded Ware people?
30760.e: Studies from 2015 onwards showed a large share of ancestry from the Pontic-Caspian steppe. The Yamnaya culture is considered the main source of it.
30760.m: The Corded Ware people carried a lot of Yamnaya steppe ancestry.

30761.q: What makes the Corded Ware graves at Eulau in Saxony-Anhalt famous?
a: They contain the oldest genetically proven nuclear family
They contain the oldest gold finds in Europe
The first wheel was found there
The oldest sky disc lay there
30761.e: DNA analyses in 2008 showed that a father, mother and two sons lay in one grave. The family was violently killed around 2600 BC.
30761.m: The oldest genetically proven family was found at Eulau.

30762.q: Where is the Corded Ware culture particularly well documented in Switzerland?
a: In lakeside settlements such as those on Lake Zurich
In burial mounds in the Engadine
30762.e: In the pile-dwelling settlements on Lake Zurich, Corded Ware pottery, wood and textiles were preserved in the damp ground. Many of these sites belong to the World Heritage Site of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps.
30762.m: In Switzerland, Corded Ware is known mainly from pile dwellings.

30763.q: Roughly how far did the area of the Corded Ware culture stretch?
a: From the Rhine to the Volga
30763.e: Corded Ware was widespread across large parts of Central, Northern and Eastern Europe. It stretched roughly from the Rhine and Switzerland to the Volga.
30763.m: Corded Ware stretched from the Rhine to the Volga.

30764.q: What was new about Corded Ware burials compared with earlier cultures in the north?
a: Single graves instead of communal graves
30764.e: Before that, many dead were laid to rest together in large stone tombs. The Corded Ware people made single graves, often under small burial mounds.
30764.m: Corded Ware relied on single graves.

30765.q: Roughly how long is the half-life of C-14?
30765.e: After about 5700 years, half of the C-14 in a sample has decayed. That is why the method is suitable for finds up to about 50,000 years old.
30765.m: C-14 has a half-life of about 5700 years.

30766.q: What does the abbreviation “BP” mean in dates used in archaeology?
30766.e: BP stands for “before present”. The present is fixed as the year 1950 so that all dates stay comparable.
30766.m: BP means before present, counted from 1950.

30767.q: How is the isotope C-14 formed in nature?
a: From nitrogen-14 through neutrons from cosmic radiation
Through the decay of uranium inside the Earth
30767.e: In the upper atmosphere, neutrons from cosmic radiation hit nitrogen atoms and turn them into C-14. This is oxidised to CO2 and so gets into plants and animals.
30767.m: C-14 forms in the atmosphere from nitrogen through cosmic radiation.

30768.q: Why do radiocarbon dates have to be calibrated?
a: Because the C-14 content of the atmosphere varied in the past
Because measuring devices become less accurate over time
Because C-14 slowly changes its half-life
Because samples absorb water during excavation
30768.e: The production of C-14 depended on things like the Earth's magnetic field and solar activity and was not constant. Calibration curves such as IntCal20, based on tree rings and other records, convert radiocarbon years into calendar years.
